3 cups water
2 tablespoons honey
1 cup queso fresco
3 tart, crisp apples, such as Crispin or Granny Smith
2 cups apple or pear cider
8 ounces piloncillo, chopped, or 1 cup dark brown sugar plus 1 tablespoon molasses
1 (3-inch) piece Mexican cinnamon
2 tablespoons butter
Pinch of salt
3/4 cup toasted pecans, coarsely chopped
Combine the water and honey in a saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the honey is dissolved and the mixture reaches 160F. Let cool for at least 3 hours or overnight. Put the honey mixture and queso fresco in a food processor and blend until smooth. Pour the mixture into a shallow nonreactive pan and put it in the freezer. Once the edges start to freeze (about 1 hour), scrape lightly with a fork, bringing the ice crystals from the edges to the center. Return to the freezer and continue scraping every 30 minutes or so, until the mixture is completely frozen and looks like small ice flakes. Meanwhile, peel the apples and dice finely. Combine the cider, piloncillo, and cinnamon in a saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the mixture comes to a boil and the sugar has dissolved. Lower the heat and simmer until the syrup has thickened and has a consistency like maple syrup. Whisk in the butter and salt. Remove from the heat and stir in the apples. Let chill to room temperature. For each serving, mound about 1/2 cup of the cheese granita into a glass or cup. Drizzle about 4 tablespoons of the apple syrup over the granita and top with 1 tablespoon of the pecans. Serve immediately.

Along Reedy River, ten miles distant, a wide pool reflects the shifting heavens throughout the year. Its sandy bottom has shifted across numerous rocks, supporting a fringe of reeds where water rats dwell and ducks nest, alongside sloping grasslands leading to gentle hills dotted with wattle trees and bluebells. Rocky Creek flows into this pool from verdant banks thick with ferns, shaded by tall, grass-covered oaks cooling the blue-toned water. 

On one Sunday afternoon, I journeyed with Mary Campbell to this expansive lagoon. We left our horses to graze as shadows lengthened on the mountainside, then walked beside Rocky Creek under the shade of the oaks. That evening, riding homeward along the river, bathed in moonlight, I spoke of our future until our tired horses drew together.  

Located ten miles from Ryan’s Crossing and five miles below the mountain top, I established a small dwelling near Rocky Creek. I cultivated the land, erected fences, and tilled the fertile soil, witnessing my initial harvest turn gold when I returned Mary to me. 

Even now, down Reedy River, the she-oaks rustle softly, mirroring the sky’s changing scenes within the pools. Sun, moon, and stars continue their eternal cycle above, while sand drifts across the stones. However, the cabin I constructed is now gone, erased by countless rains and leveled by plowed furrows. My vibrant years have faded, marked by the swaying branches of the trees and the golden wattle blooms resting upon Mary’s grave.

Synseg-Net is a novel deep learning framework that addresses the challenging task of synthetic segmentation without target modality ground truth. Instead of relying on large amounts of labeled data to train models, this approach leverages unlabeled target images and associated source images to synthesize semantic segments with high accuracy.
The framework consists of two main components: an encoder network that learns to map from src images to latent space representations, and a generator network that maps these compressed features back to dense synthetic outputs. During training, adversarial loss is applied between the real and generated output in order to optimize the model.
In experiments, we demonstrate synseg-net's ability to generate accurate segmentations for both source and target domains across a wide range of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and video analysis. These results suggest that synthetic segmentation can be achieved using only unlabeled source materials, providing valuable insights into low-resource or no-target scenarios where ground truth annotations are sparse or absent.

In 1906, the World Series pitted the Chicago White Sox against their crosstown rivals, the Chicago Cubs, who boasted an impressive regular-season record of 116 wins and a .763 winning percentage – the best in baseball at that time. Despite finishing with the lowest batting average in the American League (.230), earning them the moniker “Hitless Wonders,” the White Sox stunned the Cubs, defeating them in a six-game series. They secured victories through superior pitching in the initial matchups and better hitting later on. Games were played alternating venues, beginning with the Cubs hosting Game 1. After splitting the first four contests, the White Sox capitalized with 26 hits over the final two games. Although they averaged just .198 as a team during their championship run, this was slightly higher than the Cubs’ .196 average. Notably, White Sox pitcher Ed Walsh recorded 12 strikeouts in Game 3, surpassing the prior record of 11 held by Bill Dinneen.

Each November, Mitzvah Day International is observed globally, predominantly in the United Kingdom, as a yearly event focused on faith-driven social service. Local groups and individuals participate by volunteering their time to assist those facing needs within their neighborhoods. Through registration with Mitzvah Day, volunteers are connected with suitable projects, aiming to promote selfless acts of kindness and strengthen connections between communities while benefiting charities. Approximately 30,000 people contributed in 2013 worldwide. Originating within the UK’s Jewish community, it now extends beyond this base to encompass diverse faiths and often coincides with the beginning of UK National Interfaith Week. The Hebrew word ‘mitzvah,’ signifying “deed” or “commandment,” now commonly translates to “good deed” or “act of charity.” The most recent Mitzvah Day occurred on Sunday, November 15th, 2020.

"Public Enemies" provides a detailed and gripping account of notorious gangster John Dillinger's life, set amidst the backdrop of the Great Depression. Johnny Depp delivers an exceptional performance as Dillinger - a rather strange yet charismatic anti-hero, truly embodying the man's rebellious nature and unique charm. Christian Bale's portrayal as Agent Melvin Purvis is equally compelling, paving the way for a classic cat-and-mouse chase that forms the crux of the movie. The film also manages to weave in a touching love story that brings out Dillinger's more sensitive side.

The plot of "Public Enemies" is well-paced, managing to sustain the audience's attention through a perfect blend of action scenes and dialogues. Michael Mann's stellar direction makes full use of the film's setting, offering viewers a glimpse into the socioeconomic realities of an America in the throes of the Great Depression. The choice of a grainy, blue-toned cinematography enhances this experience, contributing to an air of gritty realism that stays with you for a while.

In terms of performance, the entire cast deserves commendable praise. However, Marion Cotillard steals the show as Billie Frechette, Dillinger's girlfriend and confidante. She brings an emotional depth to her character that contrasts well with the prevalent action-driven narrative.

One critique might be the occasional tendency of the film to prioritize style over substance, focusing more on appearances than character development. Nonetheless, this does not significantly lessen the film's overall appeal.

"Public Enemies" is a layered period drama that captivates viewers not just with its gangster theme but also with its attention to historical detail, making it a much-watched for lovers of well-crafted crime films. It carefully treads the line between glamorizing and humanizing John Dillinger, creating an intriguing character study that will leave audiences pondering on the man behind the notorious criminal.

The US economy demonstrated robust growth during the fourth quarter of 2004, increasing at an annual pace of 3.8%, exceeding initial projections of 3.1% made just one month prior. This improvement stemmed largely from increased business investment in equipment and technology, alongside a narrower-than-anticipated trade deficit. Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which measures overall economic performance, reached 3.5% – surpassing economist forecasts. Despite a strong 4.4% growth rate for the entire year (the strongest in five years) and 4% in the third quarter, rising interest rates are anticipated as a consequence, with potential increases expected on March 22nd.  Looking ahead to the first three months of 2005, economists predict continued growth around 4%, although consumer spending slowed slightly from 5.1% in the third quarter to 4.2% in the final quarter of 2004 due to a 18% jump in business spending on capital goods and software compared to 17.5% previously.

Nicobar's duty is to aid the Soviet authorities to repatriate citizens of the Soviet Union, many of whom prefer not to return to their home country. Literary activism is a form of protest and critique aimed at corporate publishing houses and the literary fiction/nonfiction that they publish. The progenitors of literary activism are the members of the Underground Literary Alliance. This group of writers is notorious for its protests, which have included making formal complaints against Guggenheim grants given to already-wealthy authors, crashing New York literary readings, and maintaining a website which reports weekly on the perceived corruption and lack of integrity of the current literary world. Acts of literary activism can also include editing and bringing out writers' work in online and print journals and through book publishers, reading and reviewing that work, writing essays about it, teaching it, talking it up, urging others to launch journals and indies presses, running reading series, laboring in arts administration, coordination innovative writing conferences, launching local writing groups, posting about authors and texts they love on their blogs or via other social networking sites.

The LPM (Landau-Pomeranzhuk-Migdal) effect is a phenomenon observed in high energy physics, where the probability of electron-positron pair production by photon-photon scattering increases with increasing photon energies. This effect has been extensively studied and modeled using various approaches, including perturbative QED and Monte Carlo simulations. In this paper, we present a new approach to studying the LPM effect in sequential bremsstrahlung processes, which involves factoring out the dependence on the photon energy from the expression for the cross section. We show that this factorization allows us to obtain analytical expressions for the cross sections at leading order in the small photon energy limit, as well as numerical results for higher orders. Our findings provide insight into the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for the LPM effect and have implications for future experiments aimed at measuring this phenomenon.

I anticipated a lighthearted film like a typical Dreamworks animated movie, just hoping for a few chuckles. However, *Kung Fu Panda* completely surpassed my expectations. While the plot is straightforward, the filmmaking is exceptional; it’s nearly impossible to fault the production. The voice acting, particularly from Jack Black and Dustin Hoffman, is fantastic, and the animation is incredibly detailed with vibrant, clear colors. The action scenes are stunningly impressive, and the humor lands perfectly. Seeing a packed theater filled with both adults and children – a truly universal appeal – demonstrated how enjoyable the film was; many people remained until the very end credits, which is uncommon these days. And, incidentally, I trust mentioning my admiration for the *Samurai-Jack*-inspired visuals doesn't reveal any spoilers.

Those critics who’ve unfairly criticized this outstanding cinematic achievement have fundamentally misunderstood its core essence.

It hardly matters that Johnny Depp’s English accent isn’t flawlessly authentic—American actors often struggle with regional dialects, and Depp’s portrayal is remarkably convincing, far surpassing examples like Keanu Reeves in *Dracula*. Considering Kevin Costner’s lackluster attempt at an English accent in *Robin Hood Prince of Thieves* illustrates my point. As a London native, I found the accent negligible compared to Depp’s strong performance.

Regarding historical accuracy, does it truly matter if the filmmakers took creative liberties? It’s a film, not a factual record. The identity of Jack the Ripper remains unknown, and the writers wisely added speculative elements to enhance engagement. I accept this approach.

Heather Graham’s excessive glamour might be noticeable, but films with substantial budgets require appealing stars. While the “tart with a heart” trope is predictable, her character functions effectively within the narrative. Compared to the exploitative depictions of prostitution in *Pretty Woman*, this film offers a more nuanced perspective.

Ultimately, the film excels due to its intelligent script, consistently impressive performances (aside from Graham), stunning visuals, meticulously crafted murders – unsettling and captivating – and an overwhelming atmosphere of oppressive darkness and profound sadness. It’s thoughtfully constructed, daringly ambitious, and avoids simplistic resolutions. This is a mature, serious film exploring uncomfortable aspects of human nature, distinct from typical Hollywood fare.

> Satyendra Nath Bose (Bengali: সত্যেন্দ্র নাথ বোস) (January 1, 1894 – February 4, 1974), was a Bengali physicist and mathematician who made contributions to quantum mechanics and statistical physics. He is best known for his work on the statistics of identical particles which are now called Bose–Einstein statistics after Albert Einstein's collaboration with him in developing this theory. This led to the discovery of the Bose-Einstein condensate, a state of matter that has been achieved experimentally since 1995.
>
> ## Early life[edit]
>
> Born at Calcutta, India, he studied at Presidency College, University of Calcutta where he obtained a master's degree in mathematics and physics in 1920. In 1936, he became professor of mathematical physics at the Indian Association for Cultivation of Science, Calcutta.
>
> ## Career[edit]
>
> His first paper on the subject appeared in 1924.^{[1]} It was sent by Einstein to Max Planck, who had developed the concept of quanta in black body radiation. Planck immediately recognized its importance and arranged for it to be published in Zeitschrift für Physik. Later, Einstein translated the paper into German himself.
>
> Afterwards, Einstein collaborated with Bose on further developments of the theory. They showed that the energy levels of photons were not equally spaced as previously thought but instead followed a discrete distribution law. This result was later confirmed experimentally by Arthur Compton.
>
> Bose also worked on the problem of the specific heat capacity of solids. He proposed a model based on the idea that electrons could move freely through the lattice structure of crystals without being scattered by impurities or defects. This model predicted that the specific heat capacity should vary linearly with temperature rather than the usual quadratic dependence observed in metals. Experimental evidence supporting this prediction was found in 1935 by John Bardeen and William Shockley using data collected by Robert Millikan

Tottenham manager Martin Jol acclaimed his players for their patience in their 3-0 FA Cup fifth-round victory over a determined Nottingham Forest side.
"We had the initiative but it wasn't easy. It was a professional sort of performance," the Dutchman said. "Forest played with a lot of players behind the ball in the first half, but at 2-0 they were dead and buried." Looking ahead to the quarter-final, Jol said: "Newcastle have got a very good side and they are always difficult." However, he added that his side, who are four places above the Magpies in the Premiership, were "not afraid of anyone". Robbie Keane, skipper for the night and scorer of the crucial second goal, echoed his manager's sentiments on the last-eight match. "They're on a high, but we're confident and in the last few games we've played well and hopefully we can go there and get the win," he said.
He conceded the win over Forest, which included goals from Noe Pamarot and Mido, was not pretty to watch. "It wasn't the best display but it's all about the result," the Irishman said. "We knew it was going to be difficult with the conditions. The pitch wasn't the best but we still tried to pass it. "We dug in and the gaffer said to us at half-time to keep being patient and that the goal will come." Forest manager Gary Megson conceded his team did not deserve anything after a poor performance. "If you play like we did and concede two goals from corners you're going to have an uphill battle against a very good team," he said. "If we defend in the Championship like we did we'll not get another point. "We were organised but I felt at times we thought the system would be enough but we didn't look like scoring."

The main character of the book is a little girl who loves pumpkins. She describes the many uses of pumpkins that she appreciates, including plastic pumpkins, pumpkins used to hold candy, jack-o-lanterns, pumpkin seeds, and her favorite, pumpkin pie. The illustrations show her and her mother traveling by car to a pumpkin patch, picking out a pumpkin, and then returning home. Along the way, they see a number of strange sights, including Frankenstein and his pet purple alligator who are returning home with their own respective pumpkins. One image shows a fantasy version of the girl's bedroom which is decorated with a pumpkin theme, including a pumpkin-themed headboard for her bed and an alarm clock in the shape of a pumpkin. The book ends with a series of pumpkin-themed puzzles that ask readers to identify a pumpkin that is different from the others, count which of a set of farmers has the most pumpkins, locate hidden pumpkins in a parade scene, and identify a pumpkin that looks like the little obese monkey in the book.

Cole advances five key arguments. Primarily, he contends that Al-Qaeda functions more like a small, isolated group than a widespread movement comparable to historical ideologies like fascism or communism. Secondly, he highlights significant segments within the Muslim world that could potentially cooperate with the United States. Thirdly, he asserts that complete energy independence for America is unrealistic. Fourthly, he suggests that Iran isn’t inherently opposed to the U.S. and warrants diplomatic engagement. Finally, Cole advocates for a phased and cautious withdrawal of troops from Iraq, avoiding abrupt departures or prolonged deployments. Drawing parallels, he compares Islamist extremists to certain American groups – portraying Salafi jihadists as akin to Timothy McVeigh and Wahhabis resembling the Amish. He emphasizes differentiating al-Qaeda from peaceful, politically active Islamic movements, much like distinctions are drawn between extremist right-wing militias and the mainstream Republican Party.

Ingredients
1/2 cup butter, melted
3 tablespoons curry powder
4 cloves garlic, minced
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper
6 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves - cut into 1 inch cubes
1 (10 ounce) package frozen peas and carrots
1 (15 ounce) can chickpeas, drained
1 (10 ounce) jar mango chutney
1/2 cup heavy cream
Directions
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). In a large bowl, mix together the butter, curry powder, garlic, cumin, salt and cayenne pepper. Add the chicken pieces, stirring until well coated with the mixture. Spread evenly in a 9x13 inch baking dish. Bake at 375 degrees F (190 degrees C) for about 30 minutes or until juices run clear when pierced with a fork. Stir in the peas and carrots, chickpeas, chutney and cream; bake an additional 10 minutes.

It’s important to address the film’s title; many devoted Harry Potter fans likely expect every review to praise it as a perfect 10/10 masterpiece. However, I won’t offer such an enthusiastic assessment as it wouldn’t reflect my genuine view. Nevertheless, “Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them” provides a genuinely enjoyable experience and is definitely recommended, particularly for those familiar with J.K. Rowling’s universe.

The performances were strong – Eddie Redmayne brilliantly portrays Newt Scamander, an unusual and reserved individual who favors animals over people. Dan Fogler’s portrayal of the muggle character was consistently amusing, showcasing his reactions to the wizarding world. Katherine Waterstone and Alison Sudol also delivered commendable performances as the two sisters involved in the adventure.

The movie’s most compelling element is undoubtedly its fantastic creatures. While the CGI might appear somewhat artificial, the inventive concepts and unique personalities of each creature elevate the visuals. Each animal possesses a distinctive trait that prevents them from seeming repetitive, and watching their capture scenes is consistently exciting.

Despite these strengths, the film does suffer from certain flaws. An excessive number of secondary characters felt underdeveloped and added little substance to the narrative (certain individuals, like Jon Voight, stand out negatively). Additionally, a significant magical threat emerges later in the film, yet it failed to fully engage me due to a lack of clarity.

Ultimately, these shortcomings don’t detract significantly from the film’s overall quality. Filled with imagination and a welcome return to the magic of witchcraft and wizardry, "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" remains a worthwhile viewing experience.

We explore several generalizations of Whitney's theorem -- a classical
formula for the chromatic polynomial of a graph. Following Stanley, we replace
the chromatic polynomial by the chromatic symmetric function. Following Dohmen
and Trinks, we exclude not all but only an (arbitrarily selected) set of broken
circuits, or even weigh these broken circuits with weight monomials instead of
excluding them. Following Crew and Spirkl, we put weights on the vertices of
the graph. Following Gebhard and Sagan, we lift the chromatic symmetric
function to noncommuting variables. In addition, we replace the graph by an
"ambigraph", an apparently new concept that includes both hypergraphs and
multigraphs as particular cases.
  We show that Whitney's formula endures all these generalizations, and a
fairly simple sign-reversing involution can be used to prove it in each
setting. Furthermore, if we restrict ourselves to the chromatic polynomial,
then the graph can be replaced by a matroid.
  We discuss an application to transitive digraphs (i.e., posets), and reprove
an alternating-sum identity by Dahlberg and van Willigenburg.

Yukos’s primary shareholder, Group Menatep, has filed a $28.3 billion lawsuit against the Russian government, equivalent to £15.2 billion.  Last year, the Kremlin forcibly sold Yukos’s key production division, Yugansk, to state-owned Rosneft for $9.3 billion to cover a substantial unpaid tax debt. Menatep contends that this seizure was unlawful and is seeking $900 million back from Rosneft for a loan Yugansk held. The Russian government justified the sale by claiming Yukos owed over $27 billion in back taxes, alleging the use of offshore entities to evade payments, leading to asset freezes and seizures. Critics allege these actions represent a deliberate effort to reassert state dominance within the energy sector. Menatep asserts the government violated the 1994 Energy Charter Treaty, issuing warnings to both the government and potential buyers of Yugansk regarding ongoing legal challenges. “The time for warnings has ended,” stated Tim Osborne, a Group Menatep director, “and we will now pursue compensation for our losses.”  Since 2003, Menatep claims its Yukos stake plummeted from $17.8 billion to almost zero – a 97% decline – resulting in a total claim of approximately $31.6 billion (including a 60% increase reflecting unrealized gains). Legal proceedings could be overseen by arbitrators in either Stockholm or The Hague. Despite signing the Energy Charter Treaty, Russia has not formally ratified it.

Formed in Washington, D.C. in 1995, The Make-Up is an American post-punk band featuring vocalist Ian Svenonius (formerly of Nation of Ulysses), guitarist/organist James Canty, drummer Steve Gamboa, and bassist Michelle Mae. In late 1999, Alex Minoff (from Golden and Extra Golden) added guitar duties until the band’s brief existence ended in early 2000. Their unique sound blended garage rock, soul, and a distinctive brand of “liberation theology,” which they termed “Gospel Yeh-Yeh.” This approach prioritized lively, interactive concerts where the audience was treated as a vital part of the performance—a “fifth member”—resulting in intensely engaging shows. Simultaneously, the band explored politically charged music rooted in communist ideals, viewing it as an opposition to prevailing capitalist rock and pop music.

A late header by teenager Danny Graham earned Middlesbrough a battling draw with Charlton at the Riverside.
Matt Holland had put the visitors ahead in the 14th minute after his shot took a deflection off Franck Queudrue. But Middlesbrough peppered the Charlton goal after the break and Chris Riggott stroked home the equaliser. Shaun Bartlett's strike put Charlton back in front but that lead lasted just six minutes before Graham rushed onto Queudrue's pass to head home. The match burst to life from the whistle and Charlton defender Hermann Hreidarsson had sight of an open goal after just six minutes. Hreidarsson received Danny Murphy's free-kick from the right but he crashed his free header wide of the far post. The Iceland international looked such a danger the Boro bench could be heard issuing frantic instructions to mark him.
Charlton's early pressure paid off when Bartlett received a long ball from Talal El Karkouri in the box and laid it off to Holland who buried his right-footed strike. Szilard Nemeth, recalled in place of Joseph-Desire Job, was twice denied his chance to get Middlesbrough back on level terms by Dean Kiely. The striker played a great one-two with Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink only to see Kiely get down well to smother his shot before directing a header straight into the keeper's arms. Boro had plenty of time on the ball but the Addicks comfortably mopped up the pressure - with Kiely tipping a Hasselbaink header over the bar - to take their lead into half-time.
It was all one-way traffic after the break at the Riverside as Middlesbrough poured forward and Kiely even saved Hreidarsson's blushes when he palmed the ball away to prevent a Charlton own goal. But the Addicks keeper could do nothing about Riggott's equaliser in the 74th minute. The Boro defender looked suspiciously offside as he got on the end of Gareth Southgate's misdirected effort, but despite the Charlton protests his goal stood. The Addicks did not let their heads drop and Bartlett left the Boro defence standing, picking up Hreidarsson's cross to easily sink his right-footed strike. But substitute Graham was on hand to grab a share of the points for the home side. The 19-year-old striker nodding home the equaliser - and his first Premiership goal - with five minutes left on the clock.
"I felt we did enough to win the game even though the first half was lacklustre. "We dominated after the break, the players showed a fantastic response and we should have gone on to win. "But for (Charlton goalkeeper) Dean Kiely, who made three tremendous saves, we could have scored five or six."
"To take the lead and then to get penned back, it feels a little bit like a defeat," admitted Kiely. "We were winning but Middlesbrough kept knocking on the door. But we stood up and credit to us we didn't capitulate. "We'll kick on now. Our short-term ambition is to progress from the seventh place finish from last year."

According to reports, Verizon secured control of US telecom firm MCI through a $6.8 billion (approximately £3.6 billion) offer, overcoming a previously higher bid from Qwest. This acquisition is anticipated to finalize on Monday, coinciding with the rapid consolidation occurring within the American telecommunications sector, exemplified by AT&T’s purchase of SBC for $16 billion earlier this year. MCI emerged from bankruptcy in April, following a collapse under the name WorldCom due to admitted accounting irregularities and fraudulent expense reporting in 2002 – resulting in shareholder losses of around $180 billion and the layoff of 20,000 employees; former CEO Bernie Ebbers faces fraud charges. Qwest has also faced scrutiny regarding questionable financial practices, including a $250 million settlement with the SEC for manipulating reported earnings. MCI holds the position of the nation’s second-largest long-distance provider behind AT&T. This merger, along with last month's $16 billion SBC-AT&T deal, represents the fifth major telecom transaction valued at over a billion dollars since October, driven by efforts to reduce costs and expand customer reach. Accessing MCI’s extensive network and subscriber base would benefit either Qwest or Verizon, mirroring the strategy employed in the SBC-AT&T deal. Given Verizon’s larger size and established mobile operations, it likely influenced the decision, with each bidder proposing a combination of cash and stock compensation.

Developed by William Alden in the 1960s, the Alden staRRcar – nicknamed “Self-Transport Road and Rail Car” – was an early concept for a personal rapid transit (PRT) system. Initially conceived as compact, electrically driven vehicles intended for local, low-speed travel within cities, it featured the option to utilize dedicated tracks for faster, long-distance journeys between cities. As one of the pioneering dual-mode vehicles, it saw both theoretical proposals and physical prototypes. Throughout its development, the design evolved significantly, shifting from a four-passenger model to a larger vehicle accommodating twenty individuals. Olivia Manning (2 March 1908 – 23 July 1980) was a British writer best known for her novel sequence The Balkan Trilogy and The Levant Trilogy, which depict the experiences of British and Romanian expatriates in Eastern Europe before and during World War II.

Manning was born in Portsmouth, Hampshire, England, and grew up in a working-class family. She attended the local grammar school and later studied art at the Portsmouth School of Art. After completing her studies, she worked as a teacher and a governess in England and Ireland. During this time, she developed an interest in writing and began to publish her short stories and articles in various literary magazines.

In 1939, Manning married the British writer and artist Reggie Smith, and the couple moved to Bucharest, Romania, where Manning's husband was posted as a British Council lecturer. It was during this time in Romania that Manning gained the inspiration for her most famous work, The Balkan Trilogy. The trilogy, consisting of the novels The Great Fortune (1960), The Spoilt City (1962), and Friends and Heroes (1965), follows the lives of a cast of British and Romanian characters against the backdrop of the political instability in Eastern Europe in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The trilogy is praised for its vivid portrayal of the social and cultural dynamics of the time and was highly regarded by critics.

Following the success of The Balkan Trilogy, Manning published The Levant Trilogy, which continues the story of some of the same characters as they navigate the turbulent events of the war in North Africa and the Middle East. The Levant Trilogy is composed of the novels The Danger Tree (1977), The Battle Lost and Won (1978), and The Sum of Things (1980).

Manning's writing is characterized by her sharp wit, keen observation, and astute understanding of human nature. Her works often explore themes of displacement, identity, and the impact of war on individuals and societies. In addition to her fiction, Manning also wrote a number of travel books and essays on various subjects.

Despite critical acclaim and a loyal following of readers during her lifetime, Manning's works did not achieve widespread commercial success. However, in recent years, there has been a resurgence of interest in her writing, with many critics and scholars recognizing her as a significant and underappreciated voice in British literature.

Manufacturers have focused on user-friendly designs incorporating rotating displays, memory card slots, and simplified controls. Furthermore, mobile companies are expanding photo sharing options through web publishing and “moblog” platforms. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are versatile tools for numerous computer vision applications. Recent progress in semantic segmentation has expanded their use to medical imaging, particularly for segmenting structures within scans. Unlike traditional CNNs that utilize 2D kernels, newer research employs 3D kernels to fully capture the volumetric information present in medical images. Despite similarities to semantic segmentation, medical image segmentation faces unique hurdles including limited labeled training data, imbalanced datasets where certain classes are rare, and the substantial memory requirements associated with 3D imagery. This study introduces a CNN approach utilizing 3D filters and tests it on hand and brain MRI scans. We explore two architectural adjustments to a standard CNN, alongside techniques designed to mitigate these challenges. Notably, this work extends beyond typical medical image segmentation research, which often concentrates on soft tissues and key organs, by validating its performance on both central nervous system and skeletal hand data.

Ingredients:
* 1 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, trimmed and cut into 1-inch pieces
* 1 tsp. kosher salt, more to taste
* Freshly ground black pepper
* 3 Tbsp. olive oil, divided
* 1 large yellow onion, diced
* 3 cloves garlic, chopped
* 1 Tbsp. fresh ginger, minced
* 1/2 tsp. ground cumin
* 1/2 tsp. ground coriander
* 1/2 tsp. ground turmeric
* Two 14.5 oz. cans diced tomatoes
* 1/2 cup coconut milk
* 2 cups baby spinach, chopped
* 2 cups green beans, trimmed and cut into 1-inch pieces
* 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, chopped, for serving

Instructions:
* Pat the chicken dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until hot and shimmering. Add the chicken pieces in an even layer and cook without moving until browned on the bottom, 3 to 4 minutes. Flip the chicken pieces and brown the other side for about 5 minutes. Transfer the chicken to a clean bowl and set aside.
* Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in the now-empty skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the onion, garlic, and ginger and cook, stirring often, until the onion is softened and translucent with some browned bits, 5 to 7 minutes.
* Stir in the cumin, coriander, and turmeric and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the tomatoes with their juice and the coconut milk and bring to a simmer. Reduce the heat to medium and cook, stirring occasionally and scraping up any browned bits, until thickened, about 15 minutes.
* Return the chicken and any accumulated juices to the skillet and stir to combine. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through, about 10 minutes.
* Stir in the spinach and green beans and cook, uncovered, until the spinach is wilted and the green beans are crisp-tender, about 3 minutes.
* Season the curry with salt to taste. Serve the curry immediately, sprinkled with the cilantro.

salt

Prepare the marinade the night before you plan to make the tamales. Chop one bunch of green onions. Mince 2 garlic cloves. Combine, then add 1 teaspoon ground cumin and 1 packet of sazon. Rub mixture all over both chicken and ribs. Place meat in separate plastic baggies to marinate in the refrigerator overnight. Next make the "hogao," a kind of sofrito. Combine chopped tomatoes, 1 bunch of chopped green onions, 2 cloves minced garlic, 1 tsp ground cumin, 1/2 packet of sazon, 1/6 cup of chopped cilantro, olive oil and salt to taste in a skillet and saute until everything is soft and tender, kind of like a mush. Cool and refrigerate until ready to assemble tamales. Now you can make the "pique" sauce. Combine 1 bunch chopped green onions, 3 cloves minced garlic, fresh lemon juice, remaining chopped cilantro, 1 teaspoon ground cumin, sugar, vinegar and salt to taste. Make this at least 2 hours before serving so flavors develop. Prepare masa harina according to package directions except use chicken broth in place of water and salt to taste. This mixture should have flavor unlike an arepa which is more bland (my husband says the masa is the best part). It should be fairly moist, but still stay together like a dough when pressed. If it is too wet you can still use it, it is just more messy. Now the hardest part is assembling them. Place about 1/4 cup of dough in the center of a banana leaf and spread it out. Put one rib and one chicken thigh piece on top. Place about 3 slices of the carrots, 6 potato sticks and 3 slices egg on top of the meat. Sprinkle with peas. Spoon 3 tablespoons of the "hogao" (sofrito) over all, then top with another 1/2 cup of spread out masa. This does not have to be uniform or even neat. Next pull up the sides of the banana leaf to form a packet. Tie with kitchen string, but do not let any of the filling seep out (I told you it was hard). If the leaves break just reinforce with extra banana leaves. Wrap packet in aluminum foil. Repeat 5 times. They are now ready to steam. Use a large Dutch oven with a steamer insert so the tamales do not touch the water in the bottom of the Dutch oven. These need to cook about 3 hours. You probably will have to replenish the water during the cooking process. Stack the tamales all the way to the top in the steamer pot and turn up the heat to high. If your pot does not hold all of them, just refrigerate or freeze the rest until you can steam them later. When you hear the water boiling furiously, turn the heat down to medium. Serve the tamales on a section of banana leaf. With the "pique" sauce on the side to be drizzled on bites of the tamale.

Let $G$ be a bridgeless cubic graph. Consider a list of $k$ 1-factors of $G$.
Let $E_i$ be the set of edges contained in precisely $i$ members of the $k$
1-factors. Let $\mu_k(G)$ be the smallest $|E_0|$ over all lists of $k$
1-factors of $G$. If $G$ is not 3-edge-colorable, then $\mu_3(G) \geq 3$. In
[E. Steffen, 1-factor and cycle covers of cubic graphs, J. Graph Theory 78(3)
(2015) 195-206] it is shown that if $\mu_3(G) \not = 0$, then $2 \mu_3(G)$ is
an upper bound for the girth of $G$. We show that $\mu_3(G)$ bounds the oddness
$\omega(G)$ of $G$ as well. We prove that $\omega(G)\leq \frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$.
If $\mu_3(G) = \frac{2}{3} \mu_3(G)$, then every $\mu_3(G)$-core has a very
specific structure. We call these cores Petersen cores. We show that for any
given oddness there is a cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph $G$ with
$\omega(G) = \frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$. On the other hand, the difference between
$\omega(G)$ and $\frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$ can be arbitrarily big. This is true even
if we additionally fix the oddness. Furthermore, for every integer $k\geq 3$,
there exists a bridgeless cubic graph $G$ such that $\mu_3(G)=k$.

Ingredients:

For the salmon:
2 salmon fillets (6-8 ounces each), preferably wild-caught and sustainably sourced
Salt and pepper to taste
For the sauce:
4 tablespoons butter
1 lime, divided
For the asparagus:
1 bunch asparagus, about 12 ounces, tough ends trimmed
1 tablespoon olive oil
Salt and pepper to taste

Instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 400 degrees Fahrenheit.
2. Prepare the salmon: Season both sides of the salmon fillets with salt and pepper. Heat a non-stick skillet over medium-high heat and add 1 tablespoon of the butter. When the butter is melted and foaming, add the salmon fillets, skin-side up, and cook for 3-4 minutes until golden brown. Flip the fillets and reduce the heat to medium. Continue cooking for 4-5 minutes, or until the salmon is cooked through. Transfer the salmon to a plate and keep warm.
3. Meanwhile, make the sauce: Add the remaining 3 tablespoons of butter to the same skillet over medium heat. When the butter is melted and begins to foam, add the juice of half the lime and a pinch of salt. Stir to combine and remove from heat.
4. Prepare the asparagus: Toss the asparagus with the olive oil, salt, and pepper on a baking sheet. Roast in the preheated oven for 10-15 minutes, or until tender and slightly charred.
5. To serve, divide the roasted asparagus between two plates. Top with a salmon fillet and spoon the brown butter lime sauce over the top. Squeeze the remaining lime half over the salmon and asparagus and serve immediately.

We study the structure of multiple correlation sequences defined by measure
preserving actions of commuting transformations. When the iterates of the
transformations are integer polynomials we prove that any such correlation
sequence is the sum of a nilsequence and an error term that is small in uniform
density; this was previously known only for measure preserving actions of a
single transformation. We then use this decomposition result to give
convergence criteria for multiple ergodic averages involving iterates that grow
linearly, and prove the rather surprising fact that for such sequences,
convergence results for actions of commuting transformations follow
automatically from the special case of actions of a single transformation. Our
proof of the decomposition result differs from previous works of V. Bergelson,
B. Host, B. Kra, and A. Leibman, as it does not rely on the theory of
characteristic factors. It consists of a simple orthogonality argument and the
main tool is an inverse theorem of B. Host and B. Kra for general bounded
sequences.

“Re-Make/Re-Model,” penned by Bryan Ferry and featured as the album’s first track for Roxy Music’s debut, begins with subtle cocktail party sounds before transitioning into the music itself. Despite a fairly simple foundation of guitar, piano, bass, saxophone, and drums, the production incorporates unusual and forward-thinking elements. Brian Eno adds persistent bursts of dissonant synthesizer noise generated by the VCS3, complementing Ferry’s intensely mournful vocals. The guitar and saxophone solos during the song's core sections often create a chaotic effect. Each instrument receives a brief solo opportunity, with the saxophone referencing Wagner’s “Die Walküre” and the bass guitar echoing the iconic “Day Tripper” riff. Notably, Phil Manzanera’s guitar playing avoids standard chord patterns, featuring solely single notes throughout, except for his solo which utilizes only chords.

To improve clustering performance, using an idealized image—rather than one with outliers, noise, or uneven illumination—is beneficial. Therefore, accurately estimating the difference (like unseen noise) between the observed image and this ideal version is crucial. We introduce an $\ell_0$ regularization-based Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm, integrating morphological reconstruction and a tight wavelet frame transform. Morphological reconstruction filters the observed image to balance detail retention and noise reduction. Combining the original and processed images creates a weighted sum, which is then decomposed via a tight wavelet frame to generate a feature set. This feature set is used within an enhanced FCM algorithm, incorporating an $\ell_0$ regularization term on the residual between the features and their ideal counterpart, leading to better residual estimation and inclusion of the ideal value in the clustering process.  Spatial information, inherent in image segmentation, is also utilized, enhancing residual reliability. To refine segmentation accuracy, morphological reconstruction smooths the clustered labels. Finally, a tight wavelet frame reconstruction uses these refined prototypes and labels to rebuild the segmented image. Experiments across synthetic, medical, and color images demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness, efficiency, and superiority over competing methods.

In this paper, we mainly study the stability of iterated polynomials and
linear transformations preserving the strong $q$-log-convexity of polynomials
  Let $[T_{n,k}]_{n,k\geq0}$ be an array of nonnegative numbers. We give some
criteria for the linear transformation $$y_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^nT_{n,k}x_k(q)$$
preserving the strong $q$-log-convexity (resp. log-convexity). As applications,
we derive that some linear transformations (for instance, the Stirling
transformations of two kinds, the Jacobi-Stirling transformations of two kinds,
the Legendre-Stirling transformations of two kinds, the central factorial
transformations, and so on) preserve the strong $q$-log-convexity (resp.
log-convexity) in a unified manner. In particular, we confirm a conjecture of
Lin and Zeng, and extend some results of Chen {\it et al.}, and Zhu for strong
$q$-log-convexity of polynomials, and some results of Liu and Wang for
transformations preserving the log-convexity.
  The stability property of iterated polynomials implies the $q$-log-convexity.
By applying the method of interlacing of zeros, we also present two criteria
for the stability of the iterated Sturm sequences and $q$-log-convexity of
polynomials. As consequences, we get the stabilities of iterated Eulerian
polynomials of type $A$ and $B$, and their $q$-analogs. In addition, we also
prove that the generating functions of alternating runs of type $A$ and $B$,
the longest alternating subsequence and up-down runs of permutations form a
$q$-log-convex sequence, respectively.

As supervised semantic segmentation is reaching satisfying results, many
recent papers focused on making segmentation network architectures faster,
smaller and more efficient. In particular, studies often aim to reach the stage
to which they can claim to be "real-time". Achieving this goal is especially
relevant in the context of real-time video operations for autonomous vehicles
and robots, or medical imaging during surgery.
  The common metric used for assessing these methods is so far the same as the
ones used for image segmentation without time constraint: mean Intersection
over Union (mIoU). In this paper, we argue that this metric is not relevant
enough for real-time video as it does not take into account the processing time
(latency) of the network. We propose a similar but more relevant metric called
FLAME for video-segmentation networks, that compares the output segmentation of
the network with the ground truth segmentation of the current video frame at
the time when the network finishes the processing.
  We perform experiments to compare a few networks using this metric and
propose a simple addition to network training to enhance results according to
that metric.

Talks aimed at averting national strikes over pension reforms have ended without agreement after 90 minutes.
Five public sector unions met Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott at the Labour spring conference in Gateshead. They want the government to withdraw regulations - due to be introduced in weeks - which would raise the pension age for council workers from 60 to 65. Up to 1.4 million workers could take part in strikes earmarked for 23 March. Discussions will resume next week.
A spokesman for Unison, Britain's biggest union, said after Saturday's meeting: "At least we are still talking." All sides are anxious to avoid a major confrontation in the run up to the general election, said BBC labour affairs correspondent Stephen Cape. In four days, Unison will start balloting 800,000 local government workers on strikes. Other public sector unions have pledged to follow. The five unions which met Mr Prescott want the government to withdraw these regulations. This would allow months of tough negotiations to follow, said our correspondent. But a spokesman for Mr Prescott warned that the changes to the local government pension scheme would have to go ahead in April.
Privately ministers believe this will be the "less painful" option, our correspondent added. The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) will co-ordinate any industrial action with up to six other public sector unions. PCS leader Mark Serwotka warned last week that there could be further walkouts unless there was a government rethink. "For a government that lectures everyone on choice - choice on public service, choice on this and choice on that - isn't it ironic that they're saying to public sector workers there is no choice," he said. "If you want the pension you were promised when you started you must work for an extra five years - that is working until people drop. "In the 20th century, it's completely unacceptable."
Unison's 800,000 workers, the Transport and General Workers' Union's 70,000 and Amicus' 20,000 are among those being balloted about a 23 March walkout. Mr Prescott held a private meeting with senior union figures last week. It is understood no deal was offered in that meeting but there was room for further negotiations.

How grace this hallowed day?
Shall happy bells, from yonder ancient spire,
Send their glad greetings to each Christmas fire
Round which the children play?
Alas! for many a moon,
That tongueless tower hath cleaved the Sabbath air,
Mute as an obelisk of ice, aglare
Beneath an Arctic noon.
Shame to the foes that drown
Our psalms of worship with their impious drum,
The sweetest chimes in all the land lie dumb
In some far rustic town.
There, let us think, they keep,
Of the dead Yules which here beside the sea
They've ushered in with old-world, English glee,
Some echoes in their sleep.
How shall we grace the day?
With feast, and song, and dance, and antique sports,
And shout of happy children in the courts,
And tales of ghost and fay?
Is there indeed a door,
Where the old pastimes, with their lawful noise,
And all the merry round of Christmas joys,
Could enter as of yore?
Would not some pallid face
Look in upon the banquet, calling up
Dread shapes of battles in the wassail cup,
And trouble all the place?
How could we bear the mirth,
While some loved reveler of a year ago
Keeps his mute Christmas now beneath the snow,
In cold Virginian earth?
How shall we grace the day?
Ah! let the thought that on this holy morn
The Prince of Peace -- the Prince of Peace was born,
Employ us, while we pray!
Pray for the peace which long
Hath left this tortured land, and haply now
Holds its white court on some far mountain's brow,
There hardly safe from wrong!
Let every sacred fane
Call its sad votaries to the shrine of God,
And, with the cloister and the tented sod,
Join in one solemn strain!
With pomp of Roman form,
With the grave ritual brought from England's shore,
And with the simple faith which asks no more
Than that the heart be warm!
He, who, till time shall cease,
Will watch that earth, where once, not all in vain,
He died to give us peace, may not disdain
A prayer whose theme is -- peace.
Perhaps ere yet the Spring
Hath died into the Summer, over all
The land, the peace of His vast love shall fall,
Like some protecting wing.
Oh, ponder what it means!
Oh, turn the rapturous thought in every way!
Oh, give the vision and the fancy play,
And shape the coming scenes!
Peace in the quiet dales,
Made rankly fertile by the blood of men,
Peace in the woodland, and the lonely glen,
Peace in the peopled vales!
Peace in the crowded town,
Peace in a thousand fields of waving grain,
Peace in the highway and the flowery lane,
Peace on the wind-swept down!
Peace on the farthest seas,
Peace in our sheltered bays and ample streams,
Peace wheresoe'er our starry garland gleams,
And peace in every breeze!
Peace on the whirring marts,
Peace where the scholar thinks, the hunter roams,
Peace, God of Peace! peace, peace, in all our homes,
And peace in all our hearts!

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation that goes beyond traditional image-based methods by incorporating contextual information from various sources. Existing approaches typically rely solely on visual cues within the image to predict class labels, which can be limited in certain scenarios, such as object occlusion or ambiguity. Our proposed method leverages additional context, including textual descriptions and spatial relationships, to improve the accuracy of semantic segmentation.

We introduce a two-stage framework that first generates region proposals using a deep neural network, followed by a novel context-aware classification module that integrates both visual and non-visual information. The contextual information is obtained through a combination of natural language processing techniques and graph-based algorithms, which provide rich semantic descriptions of the scene. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

Our key contributions include:

1. A novel context-aware semantic segmentation framework that combines visual and non-visual information.
2. An effective way to integrate natural language descriptions into the segmentation process.
3. A graph-based algorithm for inferring spatial relationships between objects in the scene.
4. Extensive experiments demonstrating the superior performance of our approach compared to traditional image-based methods.

The proposed method has important implications for real-world applications where semantic segmentation plays a critical role, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and virtual reality. By mining contextual information beyond the image, we can enhance the accuracy and robustness of semantic segmentation systems, enabling them to better understand complex scenes and make more informed decisions.

The marsh leek orchid (*Prasophyllum limnetes*) is a Tasmanian orchid species found exclusively in Tasmania. This plant features a solitary, cylindrical, green leaf and produces 15 to 35 pale greenish-white flowers accented by a pinkish labellum. Its habitat is extremely limited, consisting of under 20 individuals residing within a protected area close to Port Sorell. *P. limnetes* is a ground-dwelling, perennial herb characterized by an underground tuber and a long, tube-like leaf whose base is purplish. The leafy portion extends considerably. A slender flower spike bears these flowers, reaching a considerable height. Like other leek orchids, the flowers are upside down, positioning the labellum above the column. The dorsal sepal is elongated, approximately wide, while the lateral sepals are similarly sized but upright and separate. The petals are roughly wide and angled forward. The labellum itself is greenish-white with hints of pink or mauve, tapering to a sharp point and curving upward prominently towards its center. Its edges exhibit gentle undulations, and a prominent callus marks the tip. Blooming typically takes place between late November and December.

China's economy has expanded by a breakneck 9.5% during 2004, faster than predicted and well above 2003's 9.1%.
The news may mean more limits on investment and lending as Beijing tries to take the economy off the boil. China has sucked in raw materials and energy to feed its expansion, which could have knock-on effects on the rest of the world if it overheats. But officials pointed out that industrial growth had slowed, with services providing much of the impetus. Growth in industrial output - the main target of government efforts to impose curbs on credit and investments - was 11.5% in 2004, down from 17% the previous year.
Still, consumer prices - at 2.4% - rose faster than in 2004, adding to concern that a sharp rise in producer prices of 7.1% could stoke inflation. And overall investment in fixed assets was still high, up 21.3% from the previous year - although some way off the peak of 43% seen in the first quarter of 2004. The result could be higher interest rates. China raised rates by 0.27 percentage points to 5.8% - its first hike in nine years - in October 2004.
Despite the apparent rebalancing of the economy the overall growth picture remains strong, economists said. "There is no sign of a slowdown in 2005," said Tim Congdon, economist at ING Barings.
China's economy is not only gathering speed thanks to domestic demand, but also from soaring sales overseas. Figures released earlier this year showed exports at a six-year high in 2004, up 35%. Part of the impetus comes from the relative cheapness of the yuan, China's currency. The government keeps it pegged close to a rate of 8.28 to the US dollar, - much to the chagrin of many US lawmakers who blame China for lost jobs and competitiveness. Despite urging to ease the peg, officials insist they are a long way from ready to make a shift to a more market-set rate. "We need a good and feasible plan and formulating such a plan also needs time," National Bureau of Statistics chief Li Deshui told Reuters. "Those who hope to make a fortune by speculating on a renminbi revaluation will not succeed in making a profit."

This research examines the effectiveness of two distinct Markov field environments for pixel-based image segmentation, treating image labels as concealed states and utilizing the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) equation to estimate them. While both models share the same emission distribution, their key differences lie in the Markovian prior assumptions applied to the labeling random field – specifically, a second-order anisotropic Markov Mesh and a standard isotropic Potts model. We evaluate three segmentation approaches under these models: 2D Path Constrained Viterbi for the Markov Mesh, Graph Cut for the isotropic Potts model, and Iterated Conditional Modes (ICM) for the anisotropic Potts model.

We present a comprehensive comparison of these methods, analyzing their fit quality through various classification metrics like Overall Accuracy, Relative Improvement, and Kappa coefficient, across both synthetic and real dental radiographic data. These analyses consider factors such as parameter estimation, computational efficiency, and level of automation. Generally, the algorithms produce satisfactory segmentations when input images exhibit clear multi-modal distributions; however, suboptimal learning becomes unreliable with indistinct modes, restricting model complexity and ultimately limiting segmentation accuracy. The complete Matlab code implementing these techniques is freely available as a downloadable toolbox, adhering to the principles of reproducible research.

Robert Lee Hill (June 8, 1892 – May 11, 1963) was an African-American sharecropper from the Arkansas Delta and a political activist, founder of the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America following the Great War. Based in Arkansas, this organization was intended to help sharecroppers and tenant farmers to gain better financial arrangements with white landowners. Hill was involved in an organizing meeting of black farmers near Elaine, Arkansas on September 30, 1919. In early afternoon trade in London the company share price was down 1% at 1218 pence. "The continuing success of our key products means we can now look forward to a good performance in 2005," he said. "2005 will also be an important year in terms of research and development pipeline progress." However, the firm discontinued development of an experimental treatment for obesity, known as '771, after disappointing clinical trial results. Glaxo is relying on new treatments for conditions such as cancer, diabetes, depression, HIV/AIDS and allergies to lift the pace of sales growth after several disappointing years.

He won the prestigious Samford Fellowship, awarded by the U.S. Chess Trust to the top U.S. prospect under the age of 25, in 1999.  The fellowship granted Shahade approximately $25,000 to train for and play in top tournaments. He was also renewed for it in 2000 and subsequently scored his first Grandmaster norm at the Bermuda Closed in January 2001. Since 2006, he has held 30 sessions of the US Chess School, where the nation's top young chess talents are invited to train under the instruction of various Grandmasters.  He was the founder and Commissioner of the U.S. Chess League, which folded in 2016. His father is FIDE Master Michael Shahade and his mother was Drexel University chemistry professor and author Sally Solomon. His sister is Woman Grandmaster Jennifer Shahade.

Slouching Towards Gomorrah: Modern Liberalism and American Decline is a 1996 non-fiction book by Robert H. Bork, a former United States Court of Appeals judge. Bork's thesis in the book is that U.S. and more generally Western culture is in a state of decline and that the cause of this decline is modern liberalism and the rise of the New Left. Specifically, he attacks modern liberalism for what he describes as its dual emphases on radical egalitarianism and radical individualism. The title of the book is a play on the last couplet of W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming": "And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?" Bork contends that the "rough beast of decadence … now sends us slouching towards our new home, not Bethlehem but Gomorrah." More directly, the title borrows from Joan Didion's Slouching Towards Bethlehem. Overview
Bork first traces the rapid expansion of modern liberalism that occurred during the 1960s, arguing that this legacy of radicalism demonstrates that the precepts of modern liberalism are antithetical to the rest of the U.S. political tradition. He then attacks a variety of social, cultural, and political experiences as evidence of U.S. cultural decline and degeneracy. Among these are affirmative action, increased violence in and sexualization of mass media, the legalization of abortion, pressure to legalize assisted suicide and euthanasia, feminism and the decline of religion. Bork, himself a rejected nominee of President Ronald Reagan to the United States Supreme Court, also criticizes that institution and argues that the judiciary and liberal judicial activism are catalysts for U.S. cultural corruption.

The four Britons freed from US custody in Guantanamo Bay are expected to be allowed a visit by one relative.
Moazzam Begg, Martin Mubanga, Feroz Abbasi and Richard Belmar were held for three years, accused of al-Qaeda links. Mr Begg's father, Azmat, said he had been told he could see his son for 20 minutes and would say he was "a hero". The men are being held at London's Paddington Green police station, where they are expected to be questioned by UK anti-terror officers. But Louise Christian, the lawyer representing Mr Abbasi and Mr Mubanga, said the families would be reunited with the men away from the station. Before being driven by police from Birmingham to London, Azmat Begg said he was concerned for his son Moazzam's mental state and was looking forward to giving him a hug. As Azmat Begg arrived at the London police station, there appeared to be some confusion as to the visiting arrangements. Police have said they have a duty to investigate the men, who were arrested on their return to the UK. But Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir John Stevens said evidence obtained by MI5 while the four were in Cuba was "absolutely" inadmissible in UK courts. In an interview with the Independent, Sir John said his officers would have to find other evidence before the suspects could be tried in the UK.
He told the newspaper: "If an admission is made, it is a totally different ball game... it could be used as evidence. "The options are: if there is enough evidence they will be charged. If not they will be released as soon as possible." The men have been allowed to meet their lawyers. Louise Christian said that after being "tortured and abused" at Guantanamo Bay, the men's arrest was unfair and inappropriate. She told BBC News she remained very concerned about their psychological state. Gareth Peirce, lawyer for Mr Begg, said she was shocked at the condition of the men and appalled that the authorities felt the need to detain them. Washington has claimed all four were "enemy combatants" who trained at camps run by al-Qaeda. The Pentagon says they were freed after the UK government promised they would not be a threat to the national security of the US or any of its allies.
The detainees were immediately arrested under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 when they landed at RAF Northolt, west London, on Tuesday. Massoud Shadjareh, from the Muslim Safety Forum, said: "What sort of homecoming is this? They are innocent people." The Muslim Council of Britain urged that the men should receive counselling and medical help. "We want these men to be returned into the arms of their waiting family," said Iqbal Sacranie, secretary general of the council.

I have to say first that while I loved this movie for Cate Blanchett's great acting,for the visuals and even the soundtrack, I can't help but wonder how filmmakers can so blatantly reinvent history! I saw this movie in the theater,and had to literally bite my tongue all through it not to shout out loud at the totally fictive events, strangely telescoped time line, and juggling of names and characters.It's not like Elizabeth I is some obscure figure in English or world history. You would think SOMEONE involved in the production of this movie might have bothered to look something (anything!!)up!

I can only conclude that the makers of this film had NO intention of portraying Elizabeth's personality, intelligence, forcefulness, and political acumen accurately, let alone the events of her life and reign.The portrayal of her as faltering and weak in the beginning is hard to swallow, as she was politically subtle and well versed in the arts of intrigue from the cradle.

Although so many so-called historical films are not accurate, or portray history through a particular bias, this one must be called total fiction. It's much quicker to name the parts that ARE correct. Let's see, there was this Queen of England named Elizabeth--and..well, that's pretty much it!

They did sprinkle a lot of her famous quotes throughout, though at completely the wrong times and in the wrong situations. Alas!

And did anyone realize that the filmmakers had the wrong Duc D'Anjou? The Duc who liked to cross-dress was the older brother of the Duc who was proposed as her suitor. He had previously held that title, but was King of France at the time of his younger brother's (and present Duc D'Anjou's) suit for Elizabeth.Close, but no cigar.

I found especially ridiculous the implication at the end of the story that she was through with Robert Dudley, after his (fictional)betrayal of her. Any biography of Elizabeth is replete with references to the huge part he played in her life, both politically and personally.

I needn't go on-- I can't go on! The inaccuracies are legion, and have been mentioned in other reviews. If you don't give a tinker's damn about even approaching anything like historical accuracy, this is the movie for you. Otherwise see Elizabeth R or better yet--read a book about her.

Despite successful applications across various fields, deep learning models often encounter difficulties when trained on images containing inaccurate labels. This issue is particularly important in medicine, where reliable labeling requires specialized knowledge. Currently, there’s no simple way to mitigate the impact of poor labels without additional annotation work. Our research introduces an automated approach to evaluate label quality within deep neural networks, identifying and prioritizing accurate labels for training. The system then uses these high-quality labels to refine network parameters and incorporates an overfitting prevention mechanism to maximize learning efficiency. Evaluations on biomedical image datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to existing techniques, maintaining strong accuracy and robust generalization regardless of label noise levels.

We propose two new probabilistic generalizations of the GAN that permit segmentation networks to identify information from other information types. Our approach uses a two-stage probabilistic knowledge extraction process that can produce class-based information, and achieves a significantly more accurate and efficient probabilistic classifier than other methods we have tested. Our algorithm combines the knowledge gained in the first stage with a probabilistic model that allows us to discover class representations in a more efficient manner than any prior methods have. We applied our method to classify objects from the image of a typical flower and the image of a hand-drawn bird and to segment objects from multispectral images. All classification classes significantly improved due to this improved generalization. More specifically, there were improvements in both the class representation and in the optimal class (the class that best discriminates against most objects). In addition, our proposed probabilistic knowledge extraction can extract information at multiple discrete stages in the segmentation process.

350 grams salmon fillet
1/3 cup mild brown miso paste
2 cups vegetable stock
2 to 3 cups water, or enough to cover the fish
50 grams fresh ginger, peeled
3 garlic cloves, crushed
Soba noodles
160 grams dried soba
1 tablespoon soy sauce
1 tablespoon pure sesame oil
2 to 3 spring onions, chopped
Handful Toasted sesame seeds to garnish
Add and mix all ingredients for the poaching liquid in a pot. Bring it to a boil and turn the heat down to medium. Simmer the liquid for 5 minutes and turn the heat down to very low, as low as you can. Make sure you only see a few gentle bubbles or less and place the salmon (skin-side down if it is on). Plate the noodles and fish with chopped spring onions and toasted sesame seeds. Serve it with a bowl of miso and ginger broth you cooked salmon in.

The performance of the state-of-the-art image segmentation methods heavily
relies on the high-quality annotations, which are not easily affordable,
particularly for medical data. To alleviate this limitation, in this study, we
propose a weakly supervised image segmentation method based on a deep geodesic
prior. We hypothesize that integration of this prior information can reduce the
adverse effects of weak labels in segmentation accuracy. Our proposed algorithm
is based on a prior information, extracted from an auto-encoder, trained to map
objects geodesic maps to their corresponding binary maps. The obtained
information is then used as an extra term in the loss function of the
segmentor. In order to show efficacy of the proposed strategy, we have
experimented segmentation of cardiac substructures with clean and two levels of
noisy labels (L1, L2). Our experiments showed that the proposed algorithm
boosted the performance of baseline deep learning-based segmentation for both
clean and noisy labels by 4.4%, 4.6%(L1), and 6.3%(L2) in dice score,
respectively. We also showed that the proposed method was more robust in the
presence of high-level noise due to the existence of shape priors.

Fannie Coralie Perkins (April 10, 1880 – May 14, 1965), known as Frances Perkins, was a prominent figure in American worker’s rights advocacy. Serving as the U.S. Secretary of Labor from 1933 to 1945—the longest tenure for that role—she holds the distinction of being the first woman to join the Presidential Cabinet. A steadfast ally of Franklin D. Roosevelt, she significantly influenced the New Deal coalition by prioritizing labor concerns. Perkins remained a consistent member of Roosevelt's cabinet throughout his time in office, alongside only one other official. Notably, she spearheaded the development of the 1935 Social Security program and contributed to governmental strategies concerning labor unions, despite facing skepticism from union representatives. During World War II, her Labor Department utilized the United States Conciliation Service to resolve labor disputes, addressing challenges related to wartime employment and the increasing participation of women in traditionally male occupations. She was later featured in the documentary *Summoned* (2020).

Henshall’s *Book of Black Bass* essentially combines three distinct areas of study. Nearly 180 pages detail the biological aspects of Black Bass species prevalent during its publication.  A smaller section then addresses the specific fishing equipment needed for success, particularly notable due to Henshall’s expertise as a reel collector – his chapters on reels remain highly regarded by collectors. Finally, the third part outlines diverse fishing methods, including fly fishing. Henshall followed up with *More About the Black Bass* (1889) and a revised second edition (*Book of the Black Bass*) in 1904, incorporating material from the earlier work.  In the 1881 preface, Henshall explains the impetus behind the book: to elevate the Black Bass’s status within the realm of gamefish and foster appreciation for the species, previously hindered by inadequate tackle and limited knowledge about its behavior and worth.  The book prioritizes practicality over entertainment, lacking stylistic flourishes or anecdotal tales common in angling literature, and eschewing strict scientific rigor in favor of an angler’s perspective.

The Altiplano-Puna Volcanic Complex (APVC) comprises a series of volcanic systems situated within the Puna region of the Andes Mountains. This complex arises from the subduction of the Nazca Plate under the South American Plate, a process that generates magma and fuels volcanism along the Andean Volcanic Belt. Spanning latitudes from 21° to 24°S, the APVC covers parts of Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile. During the Miocene-Pliocene period (approximately 10-1 million years ago), it experienced four major eruptive episodes involving felsic ignimbrites from several caldera sites like Guacha, La Pacana, Pastos Grandes, and Vilama, with some events reaching a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 8. Eruptive activity decreased after about 2 million years, yet current geothermal manifestations, volcanoes active during the Holocene, and ongoing ground deformation at Uturunku demonstrate continued activity within the system today.

This paper presents a novel approach to hyperspectral unmixing using collaborative sparse regression with spatially correlated supports. Hyperspectral unmixing is a critical task in remote sensing, aiming to identify and quantify the constituent materials of each pixel in a hyperspectral image. Traditional methods often fail to consider the spatial correlation of the materials, leading to suboptimal results. To address this issue, we propose a collaborative sparse regression model that incorporates spatial correlation into the unmixing process. The model leverages the spatial correlation of the materials' distribution to enhance the unmixing performance. Experimental results on both synthetic and real hyperspectral data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in improving the accuracy of hyperspectral unmixing.

2 cups water
2 cups sugar
1 vanilla bean, split
1 (750 milliliter) bottle white rum (such as Ron Barcelo)
2 tablespoons loose Earl Grey tea
1 cup lemon juice from about 8 lemons
2 cups whole milk
2 cinnamon sticks
7 whole cloves
Combine sugar and water on medium heat until the sugar is dissolved. Remove from heat. Scrape seeds from vanilla bean into syrup and add scraped split pod. Set aside for 1 hour. Vanilla syrup can be stored in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Combine loose tea and rum in a glass container and allow to infuse for 4 hours at room temperature. Periodically shake the mixture so that it is thoroughly mixed. Strain through a fine mesh strainer and discard leaves. Rum can be stored in a sealed container in a dark, cool cabinet for up to 3 months. In a large pitcher or bowl, add vanilla syrup to infused rum and stir well to combine. Add lemon juice and stir again. In a medium saucepan heat milk, cinnamon stick, and cloves over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until it reaches 180°F (milk should be steaming with small bubbles beginning to form around the edges). Pour hot milk into the rum mixture. Set aside until mixture curdles, about 30 minutes at room temperature. Strain the mixture through a fine mesh strainer lined with several layers of cheesecloth. Do not remove the curd while straining as it acts an additional filter. Discard curds. Milk punch can be stored in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 1 month. Strain again before serving if desired. Serve over ice.

I greatly admire movies rooted in compelling true stories and executed skillfully, and “The Rookie” exemplifies these qualities. Initially seeming like a baseball narrative, it’s fundamentally about pursuing aspirations and the significance of camaraderie – baseball simply serves as the vehicle. The initial hour chronicles a struggling ten-member high school team in West Texas striving for a single victory annually, guided by their coach toward becoming district champions and competing at the state level in 1999. 

The subsequent hour unfolds from a pact between the students and their coach: if they achieve district success, he would attend a professional baseball tryout alongside them. Remarkably, his fastball dramatically increases from 85 mph to 98 mph during his transition into a 35-year-old player. The film subtly suggests a spiritual element—perhaps answered prayers to St. Rita—though the possibility remains open. Dennis Quaid convincingly portrays the character as a dedicated science teacher, inspiring coach, and ultimately, a stunned major league pitcher, culminating in his first strikeout at Arlington Stadium. While the actual Jim only played two unremarkable seasons, the focus rests firmly on his extraordinary journey and the supportive network surrounding him. 

Furthermore, the DVD boasts excellent visuals and immersive 5.1 Dolby surround sound. Supplementary materials include authentic footage of the real Jim, original clips from his past, his own narration detailing his first time on a major league mound, and insightful commentary from the director regarding several deleted scenes.
