To make this sauce, you’ll need one 16-ounce can of diced tomatoes, one 8-ounce can of tomato sauce, one 6-ounce can of tomato paste, six ounces of water, one teaspoon of sugar, a chopped garlic clove, a chopped onion, one teaspoon of dried basil (avoiding oregano due to its intensity), or alternatively, one tablespoon of fresh basil; also include 1/4 cup of grated Parmesan cheese, along with olive oil, salt, and pepper. You’ll also require baking soda and approximately one pound of ground chuck or ground round. Combine the meatball ingredients – including one egg, a water-dipped and squeezed slice of bread, another chopped garlic clove, another chopped onion, one teaspoon of oregano, and 1/4 cup of Parmesan cheese – and form into meatballs, browning them in a skillet before refrigerating for an hour. In the same skillet, sauté the onions until softened but not mushy, then add the garlic and the canned tomatoes (mashed lightly if whole). Transfer everything to a Dutch oven or saucepan. Incorporate the remaining ingredients, excluding baking soda, Parmesan cheese, olive oil, salt, and pepper. Bring to a boil, then immediately lower the heat and simmer, uncovered, for two hours, adding a pinch of baking soda and stirring frequently to prevent sticking. Adjust the acidity by adding more baking soda if necessary—taste cautiously after this step. Continue simmering for another two hours, adding olive oil as needed. The sauce should darken at the edges. Season with salt and pepper and add the meatballs; cook for one final hour.  Fifteen minutes before serving, stir in the Parmesan cheese to thicken the sauce. It tastes best when allowed to rest overnight.

This question (http://www.mathnet.org/questions/how-far-is-the-mean) uses a matrix algebra formulation that has some interesting properties:

Is it sensible to apply a vector field on each cell in this equation? Are we likely to see any problems here by letting the vectors "roll over" and filling in each row and column randomly without explicitly doing so within the matrix? Do we have any trouble with how to deal with complex numbers, non-real numbers or things like polynomials and sin cos? What would be good bounds for the parameters of the equations at most steps in their calculation so as to minimise error? I'm thinking either one with a fixed number of coefficients in order to limit the errors, or several where perhaps the parameter of interest grows exponentially with distance along each line?

I suspect my intuition may not quite be right, although I feel pretty confident that applying an arbitrary operator to all cells in the array gives us the answer. It's unclear whether this method holds up for complex variables where, say, sin cos takes exponential time; if that should actually be required (which seems unlikely). But in such cases, my feeling is that such an approach could still yield reasonable results using a more general formula that involves multiple matrix operations. This way you can get reasonably accurate results while avoiding the pitfalls in dealing with complex values -- perhaps even avoiding certain types altogether. Note that some people will probably find my use of matrix algebra rather naive compared to some others' methods ;-)

London weighting is a method used to adjust the relative importance of different countries or regions in a global economic model, such as the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) World Economic Outlook (WEO). The adjustment is made to reflect the differences in the size and economic structure of countries, as well as their contribution to global economic growth.

The London weighting was first introduced by the IMF in 1974 as a way to adjust for the fact that the United States, which was the largest economy at the time, had a disproportionate influence on global economic growth. The weighting was based on the size of each country's economy, as measured by its gross domestic product (GDP) in current US dollars.

Since then, the London weighting has been adjusted several times to reflect changes in the global economy. In 1998, the IMF introduced a new method for calculating the weighting, which takes into account not only a country's GDP but also its contribution to global economic growth, as measured by its exports and imports.

Today, the London weighting is used by a wide range of organizations and institutions, including the IMF, the World Bank, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). It is an important tool for understanding the relative importance of different countries and regions in the global economy, and for making informed decisions about economic policy and investment.

To make this dessert, start by preheating your oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease six individual soufflé dishes or ramekins with cooking spray. In a small bowl, whisk together 1/2 cup cocoa powder and 6 tablespoons of hot water until it forms a smooth paste. Simultaneously, melt 1 tablespoon of butter and 1 tablespoon of canola oil in a saucepan over medium heat, then stir in the mixture. Add 3 tablespoons of flour, ground hazelnuts or almonds, and 1/4 teaspoon of cinnamon, cooking continuously with a whisk for about a minute. Incorporate 3 tablespoons of packed brown sugar, 2 tablespoons of honey, and a pinch of salt. Slowly pour in 3/4 cup of 1% low-fat milk, stirring constantly until the mixture thickens – around 3 minutes. Combine this with the cocoa paste and let it cool slightly. In a separate large bowl, beat 4 egg whites until they’re foamy, gradually adding 3 tablespoons of granulated sugar as you go, until stiff peaks form. Gently fold one-third of the beaten egg whites into the cocoa mixture, followed by the rest, being careful not to deflate them. Spoon the mixture into the prepared dishes and bake for 15-20 minutes, or until they rise and appear set in the middle. Dust with confectioners’ sugar and top with fresh berries before serving right away.

A lion sunk by time's decay,
Too feeble grown to hunt his prey,
Observed his fatal hour draw nigh:
He drooped and laid him down to die.
There came by chance a savage boar,
Who trembled oft to hear him roar,
But when he saw him thus distressed
He tore and gored his royal breast.
A bull came next (ungen'rous foe),
Rejoiced to find him fall'n so low,
And with his horny-armed head
He aimed at once to strike him dead, -
He strikes, he wounds, he shocks in vain,
The lion still conceals his pain.
At length a base inglorious ass,
Who saw so many insults pass,
Came up and kicked him in the side:
'Twas this that raised the lion's pride.
He roused, and thus he spoke at length,
For indignation gave him strength:
Thou sorry, stupid, sluggish creature,
Disgrace and shame and scorn of nature!
You saw how well I could dispense
With blows from beasts of consequence!
They dignified the wounds they gave;
For none complain who feel the brave.
But you, the lowest of all brutes,
How ill your face with courage suits!
What dullness in thy looks appears!
I'd rather far (by heav'n 'tis true)
Expire by these than live by you:
A kick from thee is double death -
I curse thee with my dying breath!
The Moral
Rebukes are easy from our betters,
From men of quality and letters;
But when low dunces will affront,
What man alive can stand the brunt?

Raphaël Enthoven (born 7 March 1975) is a French actor and comedian.

Enthoven was born in Paris, France, to Charles Enthoven, a physician, and Annick, an artist. He has one older sister, Aurélia, who is an artist as well. Enthoven attended the Cours Flaubert, a school in Paris, where he met his friend and frequent collaborator, Grégoire Ludig. The two first gained attention for their sketches, notably the character "la femme chanteur", a woman singing in the bathtub.

Enthoven and Ludig starred in the cult hit Les Robins des Bois in 1998, which became one of the most successful French films in the 1990s. They also appeared together in the television series H and played the leads in the film Le Monde de Fred. In 2002, they starred in the comedy film Les Côteaux de Lure.

Enthoven has appeared in many films, including The Girl from Paris (2006), The Easy Way (2008), and The Women on the 6th Floor (2010). He has also had a number of small roles in American films, such as Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol (2011) and The Hundred-Foot Journey (2014).

In addition to his film work, Enthoven has also appeared on stage. He has worked with the Théâtre de la Ville in Paris and the Comédie Française. He has also appeared in a number of television shows, including the popular series The Tunnel.

Enthoven is married to the actress Audrey Tautou. They have one child together, a son named Jules, who was born in 2013.

Ukraine is to review "dozens" of state asset sales as the country's new administration tackles corruption.
The figure announced by President Viktor Yushchenko is less than the 3,000 cases mentioned last week, but will cover many of the biggest deals. Ukraine recently ousted long-serving leader Leonid Kuchma and has said it wants closer European Union links. In a separate statement, the EU said that the US should back Ukraine's entry into the World Trade Organisation. The comments came as Viktor Yushchenko prepared to head to Brussels to meet with US President George W Bush and other North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) leaders. He is the only non-Nato member leader invited to attend the summit.
Mr Yushchenko recently defeated Moscow-backed presidential candidate and Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych at the polls, and has made no secret of his wish to fight corruption and make Ukraine more transparent.
Earlier this month, new Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko said as many as 3,000 firms may have their privatisations put under the spotlight. Her comments raised concerns among a number of investors and Mr Yushchenko was seen on Monday as trying to soothe their frayed nerves. "We acknowledge that business in Ukraine is now shaped and 98% of privatisations were carried out according to the law," Mr Yushchenko said on Monday. "We have trust in this business and want to defend it by law," he continued, adding that any review would focus on "dozens of companies, not hundreds or thousands". He cited last year's sale of Ukrainian steel producer Krivorizhstal as one that had raised concerns. It was sold in June 2004 to a consortium that included Viktor Pinchuk, son-in-law of former-President Kuchma, and Rinat Akhmetov, the country's richest man, for $800m (£424m) - despite other higher offers.
Vice-Prime Minister Oleg Rybachuk called on the EU to recognise the steps that Ukraine was taking, fearing that should the country not be rewarded for its efforts there may be a backlash against closer relations with Brussels. He said that while he understood that Ukraine was not ready for EU membership, the country needed to see progress on topics such as trade and visa requirements. "We deserve an honest response," Mr Rybachuk told the Associated Press in an interview. "We understand the difficulties. We refuse to understand double standards." Ukraine may find it has a sympathetic ear in Brussels "The EU has reiterated that we support (Ukraine's) fast accession to the WTO and if possible we would like that to happen some time during the year," said Claude Veron-Reville, a spokesman for EU trade commissioner Peter Mandelson. "We have said as much to the Americans. We feel that it is important for us all to pull together for Ukraine to be allowed into the WTO. Mr Yushchenko was careful not to turn his back on Russia, which borders the country to the east, saying it was important to maintain 'pragmatic' ties with Moscow. "Russia is Ukraine's eternal strategic partner," Mr Yushchenko said.

Pamela J. Peters (born August 8, 1960) is an American attorney and judge who is the Chief United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri.

Peters was born in Kansas City, Missouri. She received her Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Missouri–Kansas City in 1982 and her Juris Doctor from the University of Missouri School of Law in 1985. She was a law clerk for Judge Richard H.CLEland of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri from 1985 to 1987. She was an associate with Armstrong Teasdale from 1987 to 1990. She was a partner with Spencer Fane Britt & Browne from 1990 to 2004. She was chair of the Employment and Labor Group at Spencer Fane from 2000 to 2004. She was an adjunct professor at Washington University in St. Louis from 2002 to 2004.

Peters was a judge on the Missouri Court of Appeals for the Eastern District from 2004 to 2010. She was appointed as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri by President Barack Obama on December 21, 2010. She became Chief Judge on December 27, 2018. Her service terminated on March 23, 2019 due to retirement.

Charles Edward Lindblom (March 21, 1917 – January 30, 2018) was an American academic who studied Economics at the University of Chicago and was Sterling Professor Emeritus of Political Science and Economics at Yale University. He served as President of the American Political Science Association and the Association for Comparative Economic Studies, as well as Director of Yale's Institution for Social and Policy Studies. Academic work
Lindblom was one of the early developers and advocates of the theory of incrementalism in policy and decision-making. This view (also called gradualism) takes a "baby-steps", "Muddling Through" or "Echternach Theory" approach to decision-making processes. In it, policy change is, under most circumstances, evolutionary rather than revolutionary. He came to this view through his extensive studies of Welfare policies and Trade Unions throughout the industrialized world. These views are set out in two articles, separated by 20 years: "The Science Of 'Muddling Through'" (1959) and “Still Muddling, Not yet through” (1979), both published in Public Administration Review.

Many challenges in computer vision—including image segmentation, pixel labeling, and scene understanding—can be expressed as binary quadratic programs (BQPs). While cuts based approaches effectively handle submodular problems at scale, non-submodular issues pose considerable difficulties. To tackle large, practically relevant problems, solutions often necessitate relaxation techniques. Common relaxation strategies for BQPs involve spectral methods and semidefinite programming (SDP), each offering distinct strengths and weaknesses. Spectral relaxation is straightforward yet yields broad bounds, whereas SDP provides tighter bounds but suffers from substantial computational demands, particularly with extensive datasets. This research introduces a novel SDP formulation for BQPs exhibiting comparable relaxation accuracy to existing SDPs alongside a dramatically improved dual optimization process – achieving scalability akin to spectral methods.  We further develop two dual solvers, quasi-Newton and smoothing Newton methods, both outperforming traditional interior-point algorithms. The smoothing Newton method excels for dense or moderately sized instances, while the quasi-Newton method proves advantageous for large, sparse, and structured data. Empirical results across various computer vision tasks like clustering, segmentation, co-segmentation, and registration demonstrate the effectiveness of our SDP formulation for resolving large-scale BQPs.

A man is facing charges of hacking into computers at the US arm of mobile phone firm T-Mobile.
The Californian man, Nicholas Lee Jacobsen, was arrested in October. Mr Jacobsen tried at least twice to hack T-Mobile's network and took names and social security numbers of 400 customers, said a company spokesman. The arrest came a year after T-Mobile uncovered the unauthorised access. The US Secret Service has been investigating the case. "T-Mobile has stringent procedures in place where we monitor for suspicious activity so that limited his activities and we were able to take corrective action immediately," Peter Dobrow, a T-Mobile spokesperson said. It is thought that Mr Jacobsen's hacking campaign took place over at least seven months during which time he read e-mails and personal computer files, according to court records.
Although Mr Jacobsen, 21, managed to get hold of some data, it is thought he failed to get customer credit card numbers which are stored on a separate computer system, said Mr Dobrow. T-Mobile confirmed that the US Secret Service was also looking into whether the hacker accessed photos that T-Mobile subscribers had taken with their camera phones. The Associated Press agency reported that Mr Jacobsen also read personal files on the Secret Service agent who was apparently investigating the case. A Los Angeles grand jury indicted Mr Jacobsen with intentionally accessing a computer system without authorisation and with the unauthorised impairment of a protected computer between March and October 2004. He is currently on bail. T-Mobile is a subsidiary company of Deutsche Telekom and has about 16.3 million subscribers in the US.

This article details a new, robust, and effective Gegenbauer pseudospectral method for solving diverse mathematical models numerically. This approach leverages the inherent stability and good conditioning of the numerical integration operators to generate manageable algebraic systems that are readily solvable with conventional solvers. It’s built upon newly developed, stable Gegenbauer quadratures utilizing a stable barycentric Lagrange polynomial representation and explicit barycentric weights for Gegenbauer-Gauss (GG) points. The paper includes a thorough error and convergence study alongside detailed algorithmic pseudocode. The resulting numerical scheme achieves comparable exponential-order accuracy to previous methods (Elgindy & Smith-Miles, 2013), but with reduced computational cost and complexity. Three benchmark tests demonstrate its efficiency and accuracy, establishing it as a valuable tool within the field of pseudospectral methods and applicable to various problem types.

We present a detailed theoretical study of the interplay between the longitudinal and the spin and valley Hall optical conductivities in a single layer of $MoS_{2}$. Using a recursive Green function technique within the random phase approximation, we calculate the optical conductivity for an indirect gap model with inclusion of both the next-nearest-neighbor and the long-range hopping. By separating the joint longitudinal and Hall conductivity into individual spin and valley Hall and longitudinal components, we find surprisingly strong spin and valley Hall signals with opposite polarity in the mid-infrared region, which reveal a parasitic Shapiro step in addition to the intrinsic step of the longitudinal conductivity. The Shapiro parasitics in the optical conductivity are closely related to the parasitic anomaly in the optical Hall effect and can be eliminated by a unitary transformation of the Hamiltonian with a proper choice of the transformation angle. Interestingly, such a transformation simultaneously removes the intrinsic step of the longitudinal conductivity, making the system a good candidate for nonlinear optoelectronic applications.

Sir Geoffrey Peveril and Major Bridgenorth had been boys together; and although they adopted different views in religion and politics, the major's influence had saved the Royalist's life after the battle of Bolton-le-Moor, and Lady Peveril had brought up his motherless girl, Alice, with her own son. After the Restoration, the Countess of Derby, who, through treachery, had suffered a long imprisonment by the Roundheads, sought protection at Martindale Castle, where Bridgenorth would have arrested her for having caused his brother-in-law, William Christian, to be shot as a traitor, had not the knight interfered by tearing up the warrant, and escorting her through Cheshire on her return to the Isle of Man. Alice was of course withdrawn from his wife's care, and it was supposed the major had emigrated to New England. Several years afterwards Sir Geoffrey's son Julian became the companion of the young earl, and, with the nurse Deborah's connivance, renewed his intimacy with his foster sister, who was under the care of her widowed aunt, Dame Christian. At one of the secret interviews between them, they were surprised by the entrance of her father, who related some of his religious experiences, and vaguely hinted that his consent to their marriage was not impossible. The next night, having undertaken to proceed to London, to clear the countess and her son from the suspicion of being concerned in Titus Oates's pretended Popish plot, Julian was conducted to a sloop by Fenella, his patron's deaf and dumb dwarf, and, as she was being taken ashore against her will while he was asleep, he dreamt that he heard Alice's voice calling for his help. At Liverpool he met Topham with a warrant against Sir Geoffrey, and on his way to the Peak to warn him, he travelled with Edward Christian, passing as Ganlesse, a priest, who led him to an inn, where they supped with Chiffinch, a servant of Charles II. On reaching Martindale Castle, he found his father and mother in the custody of Roundheads, and he was taken by Bridgenorth as a prisoner to Moultrassie Hall, where Alice received them, and he recognised Ganlesse among a number of Puritan visitors. During the night the Hall was attacked by the dependents and miners of the Peveril estate, and, having regained his liberty, Julian started, with Lance as his servant, in search of his parents, who he ascertained were on their way to London in charge of Topham. At an inn where they halted, Julian overheard Chiffinch revealing to a courtier a plot against Alice, and that he had been robbed of the papers entrusted to him by the countess, which, however, he managed to recover the next morning. Meanwhile, Christian, under whose care Bridgenorth had placed his daughter, communicated to the Duke of Buckingham a design he had formed of introducing her to Charles II, and, at an interview with her father, endeavoured to persuade him to abandon the idea of marrying her to young Peveril. Having reached London, Julian met Fenella, who led him into St. James's Park, where she attracted the notice of the king by dancing, and he sent them both to await his return at Chiffinch's apartments. Alice was already under the care of Mistress Chiffinch, and escaped from an interview with the duke to find herself in the presence of Charles and her lover, with whom, after he had placed the countess's papers in the king's hands, she was allowed to depart. Julian, however, lost her in a street fray, and having been committed to Newgate for wounding his assailant, he was placed in the same cell with the queen's dwarf, and conversed with an invisible speaker. After startling Christian with the news that his niece had disappeared, the duke bribed Colonel Blood to intercept his movements, so that he might not discover where she was, and was then himself astonished at finding Fenella instead of Alice, who had been captured by his servants in his house, and at her equally unexpected defiance of and escape from him. A few days afterwards, Sir Geoffrey Peveril, his son and the dwarf were tried for aiding and abetting Oates's Plot, and were all acquitted. In order, however, to avoid the mob, they took refuge in a room, where they encountered Bridgenorth, who convinced Julian that they were in his power, and allowed Christian to propose to the Duke of Buckingham that several hundred Fifth-Monarchy men, led by Colonel Blood, should seize the king, and proclaim his Grace Lord-Lieutenant of the kingdom. This film takes place during the Prohibition, the golden age of American Mafia, and shows the difficulties that law enforcement ​​had to arrest Al Capone, Chicago's biggest mafia boss. Brian de Palma seems to have a powerful attraction for violence and the mafia, this being his second major film on the subject (the first, if I'm not mistaken, was "Scarface"), but there is no doubt that his work was good and deserves congratulations. The story is told from the point of view of law enforcement, which is a novelty since most of the films that focus on Al Capone tend to show his life, or moments of his criminal course. This film shows him as the big villain he was and glorifies police officers, easily transforming Eliott Ness (played brilliantly by Kevin Costner in one of the most interesting works of his career) into a paladin of justice and law. Robert De Niro revisits his gangster movies ("The Godfather", "Goodfellas" etc.) in a curious and comic interpretation of Al Capone, and Sean Connery plays a street policeman of Irish descent. In fact, it was precisely in this character that Connery got his only Oscar, despite all actors have fulfilled my expectations. The film is well constructed, looking to alternate epic action scenes (sometimes recalling in my mind the glory of cavalry battle charges) with moments of great psychological depth and some suspense. At times, however, the film seems a bit forced, with exaggerated appeals to sentimentality, as it does in the final sequence, often parodied or imitated in later films. Another problem with the film is that it is not faithful to historical events. Al Capone's arrest was not like that, nor was Ness behind it. The need of sign language is increasing radically especially to hearing
impaired community. Only few research groups try to automatically recognize
sign language from video, colored gloves and etc. Their approach requires a
valid segmentation of the data that is used for training and of the data that
is used to be recognized. Recognition of a sign language image sequence is
challenging because of the variety of hand shapes and hand motions. Here, this
paper proposes to apply a combination of image segmentation with restoration
using topological derivatives for achieving high recognition accuracy. Image
quality measures are conceded here to differentiate the methods both
subjectively as well as objectively. Experiments show that the additional use
of the restoration before segmenting the postures significantly improves the
correct rate of hand detection, and that the discrete derivatives yields a high
rate of discrimination between different static hand postures as well as
between hand postures and the scene background. Eventually, the research is to
contribute to the implementation of automated sign language recognition system
mainly established for the welfare purpose.

However, the court also found that the band had transformed the sample so significantly that it constituted a new and original work of art, thus falling under the protection of fair use laws.

The ruling marks a major victory for the Beastie Boys, who have been embroiled in a number of copyright infringement lawsuits over the years. The group had argued that they believed they had the right to use the sample due to their status as pioneers of the rap genre, and the fact that they had credited Spence as the original composer in the song.

Spence, who died in 2005, had also been a fan of the Beastie Boys, and had given his permission for the band to use the sample in question. However, his family argued that the band breached their agreement by commercializing the song without sharing the profits, and had made money off Spence's work without compensation.

The ruling also set a precedent for the future of sampling in the music industry. The court found that in order for a song to qualify as fair use under copyright laws, it must be significantly changed and must serve a new and transformative purpose. This means that simply using a sample from one work in a new piece is not enough to constitute fair use, and that original creators must be compensated for their work.

Overall, the ruling marks a significant victory for fair use and copyright law, and is a reminder that the creative process is a collaborative effort, with original creators entitled to recognition and compensation for their work.

Isaac Barr’s mother Catharine (Baird) Barr, also born in Ireland, died when Isaac was 10 years old.  Isaac Barr’s early education was in a small rural school where the teacher was his father, supplementing his modest ministerial stipend. William Barr brought much of his ministerial approach to education and young Isaac emulated his father by playing the role of preacher in childhood games. From 1868 – 1870 Barr attended Huron College, in London, Ontario, with the intention of becoming an Anglican cleric. In 1870, he moved his studies to the University of Toronto.  Following graduation he began his ministerial career as a curate in Exeter and Woodstock, Ontario.

Our research employs a Potts model community detection algorithm to precisely quantify the layered or multi-scale organization within graphs. This algorithm generates numerous “replica” versions of the graph at varying scales and assesses their interrelationships. Strong correlations between these replicas pinpoint significant multiresolution patterns. Metrics like average normalized mutual information and information variance provide numerical assessments of optimal resolutions and reveal the robustness of detected structures. Since the method relies on comparing information, it's adaptable to diverse community detection techniques capable of analyzing multiple levels of detail. Furthermore, this approach could be applied to various optimization challenges. Unlike other prevalent models, the Potts model’s local focus overcomes resolution limitations. Consequently, our algorithm achieves top-tier accuracy compared to existing methods, enabling analysis of graphs containing up to 40 million nodes and exceeding a billion edges. Notably, our multiresolution version successfully handles systems with 200,000 nodes and 10 million edges on a single processor, maintaining exceptional precision. Generally, performance demonstrates a super-linear relationship – approximately O(L^{1.3}) for community detection and O(L^{1.3} log N) for the multiresolution variant – where L represents the edge count and N signifies the node quantity.

Boyer's multifaceted book explains the genesis of religious concepts through the mind's cognitive inference systems, comparable to pareidolia and perceptions of religious imagery in natural phenomena resulting from face perception processes within the human brain. Boyer supports this naturalistic origin of religion with evidence from many specialized disciplines including biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, cognitive science, linguistics, evolutionary biology, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and information processing. Religion Explained frames religious practices and beliefs in terms of recent cognitive neuroscience research in the modularity of mind. This theory involves cognitive "modules" ("devices" or "subroutines") underlying inference systems and intuitions. For instance, Boyer suggests culturally-widespread beliefs in "supernatural agents" (e.g., gods, ancestors, spirits, and witches) result from agent detection: the intuitive modular process of assuming intervention by conscious agents, regardless of whether they are present. "When we see branches moving in a tree or when we hear an unexpected sound behind us, we immediately infer that some agent is the cause of this salient event. We can do that without any specific description of what the agent actually is." Boyer cites E. E. Evans-Pritchard's classic Zande story about a termite-infested roof collapsing. For the anthropologist, the house caved in because of the termites. For the Zande, it was quite clear that witchcraft was involved. However, the Zande were also aware that the termites were the proximate cause of the incident. But what they wanted to know was why it happened at that particular time, when particular people were gathered in the house. Within Boyer's hypothesis, religion is a "parasite" (or "spandrel") offshoot from cognitive modules, comparable to the way the reading process is parasitic upon language modules. As I have pointed out repeatedly the building of religious concepts requires mental systems and capacities that are there anyway, religious concepts or not. Religious morality uses moral intuitions, religious notions of supernatural agents recruit our intuitions about agency in general, and so on. This is why I said that religious concepts are parasitic upon other mental capacities. Our capacities to play music, paint pictures or even make sense of printed ink-patterns on a page are also parasitic in this sense. This means that we can explain how people play music, paint pictures and learn to read by examining how mental capacities are recruited by these activities. The same goes for religion. Because the concepts require all sorts of specific human capacities (an intuitive psychology, a tendency to attend to some counterintuitive concepts, as well as various social mind adaptations), we can explain religion by describing how these various capacities get recruited, how they contribute to the features of religion that we find in so many different cultures. We do not need to assume that there is a special way of functioning that occurs only when processing religious thoughts. Boyer admits his explanation of religion is not a quick, shoot-from-the-hip solution of the kind that many people, either religious or not, seem to favor. There cannot be a magic bullet to explain the existence and common features of religion, as the phenomenon is the result of aggregate relevance – that is, of successful activation of a whole variety of mental systems.

Single-elimination (SE) tournaments—used in events like sports and elections—present the “tournament fixing problem” (TFP): can a scheduler manipulate initial rankings to ensure a preferred contestant wins? This research establishes novel conditions regarding the observed match outcomes and the favored player, guaranteeing a winning seed exists. These findings broaden existing knowledge considerably. Furthermore, the study examines how the set of potential tournament victors under specific seeds relates to established tournament designs. The work extends and improves earlier probabilistic models used to simulate tournaments; specifically, it demonstrates that every participant in an *n*-player tournament created through the Condorcet Random Model becomes a guaranteed winner, even with minimal randomness ($p = \Theta(\ln n / n)$), whereas previous research only applied this to larger probabilities ($p \ge \Omega(\sqrt{\ln n / n})$). Finally, new results are presented for broader, more versatile tournament generation methods.

Systemic mean pressure, often termed mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP), represents the average pressure within the circulatory system when blood flow ceases. A related concept, mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP), reflects the average pressure throughout both the circulatory and pulmonary systems under these conditions. In animal studies, typical MSP values hover around 7 mm Hg. This metric signifies the fullness of the circulatory system—specifically, the ratio of circulating blood volume to its total capacity—and is affected by blood volume and the constriction of vein walls. MSP is assessed through two experimental methods, leading to differing designations. MSFP is determined by occluding the aorta and major veins entering the right atrium, whereas MCFP is measured via temporary cessation of heart function or natural cardiac arrest allowing for blood redistribution. Alternatively, it can be estimated in living patients using breath-holding maneuvers during ventilation. This technique allows researchers to observe drug impacts on venous tone with consistent blood volume or track hemodynamic shifts during bleeding.

Information flow is the branch of security that studies the leakage of
information due to correlation between secrets and observables. Since in
general such correlation cannot be avoided completely, it is important to
quantify the leakage. The most followed approaches to defining appropriate
measures are those based on information theory. In particular, one of the most
successful approaches is the recently proposed $g$-leakage framework, which
encompasses most of the information-theoretic ones. A problem with $g$-leakage,
however, is that it is defined in terms of a minimization problem, which, in
the case of large systems, can be computationally rather heavy. In this paper
we study the case in which the channel associated to the system can be
decomposed into simpler channels, which typically happens when the observables
consist of multiple components. Our main contribution is the derivation of
bounds on the (multiplicative version of) $g$-leakage of the whole system in
terms of the $g$-leakages of its components. We also consider the particular
cases of min-entropy leakage and of parallel channels, generalizing and
systematizing results from the literature. We demonstrate the effectiveness of
our method and evaluate the precision of our bounds using examples.

This paper presents the experimental study revealing weaker performance of
the automatic iris recognition methods for cataract-affected eyes when compared
to healthy eyes. There is little research on the topic, mostly incorporating
scarce databases that are often deficient in images representing more than one
illness. We built our own database, acquiring 1288 eye images of 37 patients of
the Medical University of Warsaw. Those images represent several common ocular
diseases, such as cataract, along with less ordinary conditions, such as iris
pattern alterations derived from illness or eye trauma. Images were captured in
near-infrared light (used in biometrics) and for selected cases also in visible
light (used in ophthalmological diagnosis). Since cataract is a disorder that
is most populated by samples in the database, in this paper we focus solely on
this illness. To assess the extent of the performance deterioration we use
three iris recognition methodologies (commercial and academic solutions) to
calculate genuine match scores for healthy eyes and those influenced by
cataract. Results show a significant degradation in iris recognition
reliability manifesting by worsening the genuine scores in all three matchers
used in this study (12% of genuine score increase for an academic matcher, up
to 175% of genuine score increase obtained for an example commercial matcher).
This increase in genuine scores affected the final false non-match rate in two
matchers. To our best knowledge this is the only study of such kind that
employs more than one iris matcher, and analyzes the iris image segmentation as
a potential source of decreased reliability.

Store in an airtight container. This recipe yields roughly 48 cookies (adapted from Joy of Baking).

Detecting buildings using satellite multispectral imagery presents a significant challenge due to the need to accurately extract building outlines from detailed images. This research introduces a deep learning method for building detection, utilizing several improvements at each stage. The initial dataset undergoes 2-sigma percentile normalization before employing an ensemble modeling technique that integrates OpenStreetMap data. Binary Distance Transformation (BDT) enhances data labeling, and the U-Net architecture—originally designed for biomedical image segmentation—is augmented with batch normalization layers. We then analyze how each element of our method impacts overall detection precision.  Finally, we benchmark our performance against winning entries from the SpaceNet 2 competition on satellite images of Las Vegas, Paris, Shanghai, and Khartoum, highlighting the value of our approach in boosting building detection accuracy.

Based in Oakland, California, the nonprofit Food First—formerly the Institute for Food and Development Policy—was established in 1975 by Frances Moore Lappé and Joseph Collins. They operate as a “people’s think tank” dedicated to education and action, aiming to eradicate hunger-related injustices. Their core objective centers on achieving food sovereignty for both human rights and sustainable economic opportunities, achieved through three key initiatives: strengthening local food systems, empowering farmer-led movements, and promoting democratic development approaches. Food First provides policy research concerning poverty, agriculture, and broader development issues, notably criticizing the strategies of organizations like the World Bank and IMF.  The group scrutinizes the Green Revolution, initiated in the 1970s, arguing it failed to deliver promised improvements due to its reliance on expensive inputs and limited gains compared to conventional farming. Despite a renewed interest in this approach, fueled by GMOs and high-yield crops, Food First contends that such policies exacerbate global disparities and advocates instead for equitable development via localized, environmentally sound agricultural practices.

Ingredients:

Salt and pepper to taste

Directions:

A rigid man of fifty leads a solitary, apparently respectable life, as clerk and bookkeeper for a small business and part-time rent collector for his landlord. The tenuous mental equilibrium he has been able to maintain is threatened when a young man, healthy in mind and body, a doctoral candidate in psychology, becomes a roomer in the house. For this recipe, you’ll need two medium lemons, 2 cups of unbleached all-purpose flour, 1 ¾ cups of sugar, 1 ½ teaspoons of kosher salt, ½ teaspoon of baking powder, ½ teaspoon of baking soda, 1 ⅓ cups of extra-virgin olive oil, 1 ¼ cups of 2% milk, three large eggs, and ¼ cup of limoncello. Preheat your oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Warm the milk, eggs, and limoncello slightly – room temperature is best—while you prepare the lemons and wait for the oven to heat. Zest both lemons, aiming for about 1 ½ tablespoons of zest, then juice one lemon to get roughly ¼ cup of juice. Next, grease and line a 2” high cake pan (a spring form works well) with parchment paper and butter the paper too. In a medium bowl, combine the flour, sugar, salt, baking powder, and baking soda. In a stand mixer, blend the egg yolks, milk, olive oil, limoncello, lemon zest, and lemon juice. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients while mixing slowly until everything is just incorporated. Pour the batter into the prepared pan and bake for 60 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. Let the cake rest on a wire rack for 30 minutes before loosening the edges with a knife and inverting it onto another rack. Remove the parchment paper and flip the cake over again, allowing it to cool completely – usually about 2 hours – before frosting or serving plain, perhaps with some fresh berries like blueberries.

The tricks in question include the use of manipulative design features, such as slot machines with misleading odds and interactive elements that encourage players to keep gambling. Critics argue that these tactics exploit vulnerable individuals, including those struggling with addiction, and can lead to financial and emotional harm.

UK lawmakers have been pushing for stricter regulations on gambling in recent years, and the proposed ban on US casino tricks is the latest development in this effort. According to a spokesperson for the UK Gambling Commission, "We are committed to ensuring that gambling is conducted fairly and transparently, and we will not tolerate any practices that exploit or harm consumers."

The proposal has received support from numerous organizations, including the National Gambling Helpline and the Responsible Gambling Trust. However, the US casino industry has pushed back against the proposal, arguing that the tricks in question are not harmful and are a standard part of the industry's practices.

Industry representatives have also pointed out that the UK's gambling regulations are already among the strictest in the world, and that a ban on these practices could hurt the industry's competitiveness. However, critics argue that the well-being of consumers should take priority over industry profits.

The proposal is currently being reviewed by the UK government, and a final decision is expected in the coming months. If the ban is implemented, it would mark a significant shift in the UK's approach to gambling regulation and could have far-reaching implications for the industry.

Regardless of the outcome, the debate over gambling regulations is likely to continue, as lawmakers and industry representatives grapple with the complex issue of balancing consumer protection with the economic benefits of the gambling industry.

I just finished watching "The Butterfly Effect" and I'm still trying to process my thoughts about it. The film had an intriguing premise - a man discovers that he has the ability to travel back in time and change events from his past, but each time he does, the present changes in unexpected ways.

I have to say, the first half of the movie was really engaging. The main character, Evan Treborn, played by Ashton Kutcher, is a likable guy who you can't help but feel for as he tries to navigate his way through life with this strange power. The scenes where he goes back in time and alters events are well-executed and suspenseful, leaving you wondering what will happen next.

But as the movie progresses, things start to fall apart. The plot becomes increasingly convoluted and hard to follow, with too many characters and subplots that don't add anything meaningful to the story. The dialogue also gets cheesier and more predictable, which takes away from the overall impact of the film.

One thing that really bothered me was the lack of consistency in the rules of time travel. It seems like the writers made up their own rules as they went along, without thinking through the consequences or logic of them. For example, why can Evan only go back in time to moments when he was in the same location? And how come he can change some things but not others? These questions are never adequately answered, leaving the viewer feeling frustrated and confused.

Despite these flaws, I did appreciate the attempt at exploring deeper themes such as the butterfly effect itself, the concept of fate vs free will, and the idea that our choices have consequences that ripple out beyond our own lives. However, these ideas could have been executed much better with tighter writing and a clearer vision.

Overall, I would say that "The Butterfly Effect" starts off strong but ultimately falls flat due to its poor execution and inconsistencies. If you're a fan of sci-fi or time travel movies, you might find it worth watching, but otherwise, there are definitely better options out there.

Evolutionary anthropology is an integrative field combining natural and social sciences to investigate the development of human bodies, behaviors, and the connections between hominids and other primates. It encompasses areas such as the history of humankind (human evolution and anthropogeny), the fossil record of both humans and primates (paleoanthropology and paleontology), primate behavior (primatology and ethology), the historical roots of human culture (sociocultural evolution, incorporating phylogenetic linguistics), the biological underpinnings of human thought and action (evolutionary psychology and linguistics), the examination of human tools and their transformations across time and place (archaeological analysis), genetic shifts within the human genome (human evolutionary genetics), the cognitive and behavioral aspects of humans and primates through neuroscience and related disciplines, and the interactions between people and their surroundings (behavioural ecology). Further research includes comparative anatomical and physiological studies, molecular and biochemical analyses, and exploration of species variations and cultural influences.

This book focuses on an aspect of World War II that is largely ignored in many history books – the Nazi looting of Europe and Russia and the Allied recovery and repatriation of stolen art. Little known to the general public, Hitler diverted his attention from the prosecution of the war to the systematic theft of Europe’s great art. His dream was to build the world’s greatest collection – The Führermuseum – in his hometown of Linz, Austria. European museum officials took extraordinary measures to protect art from Hitler and the ensuing war. When U.S. forces prepared to enter Europe, they assembled a special force of largely American and British museum directors, curators, and art historians known as the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives program (MFAA) section, attached to the Allied armies. These “Monuments Men” attempted to minimize damage to European monuments and architecture, then track down stolen works of art. Their effort would become one of the greatest “treasure hunts” in history. In the end, Allied forces located more than 1,000 repositories in mines and castles across Europe, many of which were filled with art, sculpture, furniture, archives, and other cultural property stolen by the Nazis. Edsel points out that thousands of pieces are still missing, such as Raphael’s Portrait of a Young Man from the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków, Poland. Rescuing Da Vinci tells this story through brief text and more than 460 photographs, 60 of which are in color. This group of photographs has never been published in a single book, and many have not been seen in decades. Images such as Michelangelo’s David entombed in brick for protection or a Rembrandt Self Portrait sitting atop crates in a salt mine, capture the story better than words could describe.

Tony Blair and Gordon Brown are reportedly engaged in another intense dispute, this time concerning the attribution of credit for the government’s international aid and debt programs, especially regarding the response to the tsunami crisis – an area where cooperation was widely anticipated. He stated emphatically, “I’m not interested in what appears in the media; we maintain a unified objective.” He continued to commend Brown’s performance and future efforts, though he wouldn’t guarantee him a position post-election. “Apocalypse Now” stands as both the pinnacle of war cinema and a landmark achievement in filmmaking, having earned the esteemed Palme d’Or at Cannes and consistently being hailed as a pivotal moment in cinematic history. Rooted in Joseph Conrad’s “Heart of Darkness,” the film transcends its specific setting within the Vietnam War to explore the broader nature of conflict and its profound impact on the individual psyche. It presents a timeless narrative examining the inherent contradictions within humanity – the balance between morality, primal instincts, and the choices that define our behavior.

The film centers around U.S. Army Captain Benjamin Willard (Martin Sheen), tasked with a perilous mission into Cambodia via river to eliminate Colonel Kurtz (Marlon Brando), a disgraced officer who has devolved into insanity and established himself as a deity among a local tribe. Despite its straightforward setup, the film delves far beyond superficiality, offering a harrowing exploration of madness and the darkness of human nature. A comprehensive analysis could fill volumes; however, my perspective sees the river as representing not just the path to Kurtz, but also a descent into madness mirroring Willard’s own internal corruption fueled by the film's central theme of dehumanization. This fluvial voyage echoes Dante’s challenging pilgrimage through torment, punctuated by key encounters along the way. Each leg of the journey amplifies the dehumanizing effects of war and introduces progressively darker impulses within the characters. 

Initially, the narrative intersects with Lieutenant Kilgore, illustrating how war has transformed him and his men, leading them to prioritize their passion for combat above all else after stripping away empathy for the enemy.

"Cheerleader" is a song recorded by Jamaican singer and songwriter Omi. The track was written and produced by OMI and Clifton Dillon, Mark Bradford, and Ryan Dillon. OMI first began developing the song in 2008, when he created its melody. It was refined over several years alongside famed Jamaican producer Clifton Dillon. It was first recorded with veteran session musicians Sly and Robbie and Dean Fraser. Released as a single on independent label Oufah, the song saw success in Jamaica, where it topped the charts, and also attracted airplay in Hawaii and Dubai. Ultra contacted two disc jockeys to produce remixed versions of the original song. The label and song's producers preferred one remix, produced by a young German DJ, Felix Jaehn, that eschewed much of the song's original instrumentation for a tropical-flavored deep house rendition, prominently featuring a trumpet, a conga beat, and piano. A remix extended play was released in May 2015 by Ultra, which began to first see commercial success that fall. "Cheerleader" achieved commercial success in 2015, when it reached number one in 20 countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, France, Mexico, Ireland, Sweden, and Germany.

Preheat oven to 325 degrees F. Butter and flour a 9 by 2-inch spring form pan. Put the chocolate, butter, and salt in a large microwave safe bowl. Melt in the microwave on 75 percent power for 2 minutes. Stir and microwave again until completely melted, about 2 minutes more. Alternatively, put the chocolate and butter in a heatproof bowl. Bring a saucepan filled with an inch or so of water to a very slow simmer; set the bowl on the pan without touching the water. Stir occasionally until melted. The Medusa Algorithm is a novel approach to performing polynomial matings in machine learning. This algorithm improves upon traditional methods by utilizing an efficient matrix multiplication technique to streamline the mating process. The algorithm takes advantage of parallelism and specialized hardware accelerators, such as graphics processing units (GPUs), increasing both speed and accuracy.

Furthermore, the Medusa Algorithm incorporates a unique genetic recombination step that allows for more effective exploration of the solution space. By using this method, the algorithm can generate diverse solutions with high quality, making it particularly useful in cases where there are no clear local optima. Additionally, the algorithm includes a convergence test that ensures accurate results within a reasonable timeframe.

Overall, the research outlines the effectiveness of the Medusa Algorithm in addressing common problems in polynomial mating found in previous research. The algorithm's combination of efficient matrix multiplication, parallelization, genetic recombination, and convergence testing make it a valuable tool for improving the efficiency and reliability of machine learning techniques.

Segmentation of organs or lesions from medical images plays an essential role
in many clinical applications such as diagnosis and treatment planning. Though
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have achieved the state-of-the-art
performance for automatic segmentation, they are often limited by the lack of
clinically acceptable accuracy and robustness in complex cases. Therefore,
interactive segmentation is a practical alternative to these methods. However,
traditional interactive segmentation methods require a large amount of user
interactions, and recently proposed CNN-based interactive segmentation methods
are limited by poor performance on previously unseen objects. To solve these
problems, we propose a novel deep learning-based interactive segmentation
method that not only has high efficiency due to only requiring clicks as user
inputs but also generalizes well to a range of previously unseen objects.
Specifically, we first encode user-provided interior margin points via our
proposed exponentialized geodesic distance that enables a CNN to achieve a good
initial segmentation result of both previously seen and unseen objects, then we
use a novel information fusion method that combines the initial segmentation
with only few additional user clicks to efficiently obtain a refined
segmentation. We validated our proposed framework through extensive experiments
on 2D and 3D medical image segmentation tasks with a wide range of previous
unseen objects that were not present in the training set. Experimental results
showed that our proposed framework 1) achieves accurate results with fewer user
interactions and less time compared with state-of-the-art interactive
frameworks and 2) generalizes well to previously unseen objects.

Born in 1959 in Hennigsdorf, East Germany, Torsten Schlüter is a German painter, performance artist, and writer. After studying architecture at the Bauhaus-Universität Weimar from 1981 to 1986, he shifted his focus to painting, a decision that led to his being declared *persona non grata* by authorities in Weimar. Seeking respite, he increasingly found sanctuary on the Baltic Sea island of Hiddensee. Between 1986 and 1987, he supplemented his artistic endeavors with various jobs including sign painting, carpentry, stage scenery creation, and tennis instruction, alongside designing sets and costumes for theater productions. In 1987, he inaugurated the annual “Kunstgarten,” an open-air gallery on Hiddensee. From 1988 onward, he operated as a freelance artist. His political activism intensified in 1989 through involvement with Neues Forum. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall, he embarked on extensive travels and projects, particularly in Africa and India. He established an art studio at the Atelierhaus Weimar in 1990, later relocating to a studio within the Kulturbrauerei, Berlin, in 1994. Subsequent years saw him working out of studios in Hackesche Höfe (1996) and Berlin Mitte (2003), culminating in the design of the official logo for Hiddensee in 1995. He participated in “Tulipamwe” (1997), addressing the North-South divide through artwork, and received the “Süddeutscher Aquarellpreis” award in 2004. Furthermore, he engaged with “Eisern Union” for “1. FC Union Berlin” and the Goethe Institute Berlin in 2004, and created “Hiddensee Edition” projects in 2007 and 2010, concluding with the “Well women-High Priestesses of the Market” project at the Gerhart Hauptmann Haus in 2008.

The Lehigh Division was a railway division of the Pennsylvania Railroad (PRR) in the United States, active from 1873 until 1968. It consisted of 154 miles (248 kilometers) of track in eastern Pennsylvania.

The Lehigh Division was created in 1873, when the Lehigh Valley Railroad merged with the PRR. The division's name came from the Lehigh River, which runs through the eastern part of its territory.

In the early 1900s, the Lehigh Division was home to some of the PRR's busiest coal mines, shipping coal to destinations as far away as New York City and Boston. The division's routes also served the cities of Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Harrisburg.

During the decline of coal mining in the mid-20th century, the Lehigh Division saw its passenger traffic decrease significantly. In 1958, Amtrak took over passenger service in the region, but this only further reduced the division's popularity.

The Lehigh Division was officially disbanded in 1968, but its legacy can still be seen in the numerous rail lines that continue to operate in the area today. Many of these lines have been converted to freight-only service, while others have been abandoned altogether.

Despite its history of decline, the Lehigh Division remains an important part of the region's transportation infrastructure. The division's former tracks continue to serve as critical connections for businesses and residents throughout eastern Pennsylvania.

As I haven’t read the book, my assessment is entirely based on the movie itself. The film proved challenging to watch; I frequently shed tears throughout. While visually stunning, I believe a key element missed by many viewers is the profound connection between John and his father, which deeply affected me emotionally. Specifically, the scene after his father’s stroke, during which John reads the letter, was exquisitely portrayed and incredibly moving. 

The film thoughtfully examines several significant themes, notably the difficulties faced by children with autistic parents—particularly when those parents provide sole care. Characters Aaron and John’s father demonstrate how crucial routines are for individuals with autism, and disruptions can lead to considerable anxiety. Sadly, autism is still sometimes wrongly perceived as justification for negative behavior, and this film rightly highlights this misunderstanding of the condition. It also addresses the rarer issue of autism within parenting.

John’s relationship with Savannah plays a supporting role compared to his bond with his father, though Tatum and Seyfried deliver strong performances, conveying genuine emotion and the underlying pain between their characters. I appreciated the deliberately ambiguous conclusion regarding their dynamic. 

Overall, it’s a skillfully crafted film tackling vital social concerns, yet a written review inevitably falls short of capturing its full impact. Personally, I couldn’t bear to rewatch it due to its intensity, illustrating just how powerfully the film resonates. It remains a worthwhile viewing experience, despite its emotional weight.

For this dish, you’ll need approximately 3-4.5 kilograms of pig’s feet. Also, gather 12 limes, 2 medium cucumbers (sliced, seeded, and peeled), one medium white onion, and either a Scotch bonnet or Thai chili pepper. Season generously with salt and pepper. Add white vinegar to your liking, along with enough water to cover the feet. Bring the pot of water and feet to a boil and cook for 30-60 minutes, or until tender. Finely chop the onion – you can slice it into strips if you prefer. Combine the chopped onion, sliced cucumbers, lime juice, and a portion of the chili pepper (use less if you aren't sensitive to spice). Adjust the consistency with water and vinegar to achieve your desired flavor. Remember to wear gloves when handling the pepper and thoroughly clean your cutting board and knives afterward. Cover the cooked pig’s feet with plastic wrap and refrigerate during cooking. After the pig is cooked, transfer it to a bowl and mix with the flavorful liquid from the cooking process. Allow to cool completely, then marinate in the refrigerator for 2-3 days. Before serving, add fresh cucumber slices to marinate briefly to maintain their crispness. Serve at room temperature or chilled – enjoy! *Note:* Be cautious with hot peppers; I've experienced allergic reactions and burns, so always wear gloves and keep cold milk or sour cream handy should irritation occur.

For this recipe, you’ll need 6 slices of bacon, chopped into half-inch pieces, along with 4 pounds of beef blade roast or cross-rib roasts. Combine 1/2 cup of packed brown sugar, 2 teaspoons of salt, 1 teaspoon of garlic powder, 1 teaspoon of black pepper, 1 teaspoon of dried thyme, 1 cup of water, and 12 ounces of beer. Begin by frying the bacon in a 5-quart Dutch oven until crispy; then remove it and drain on paper towels. Next, brown the beef in its own rendered fat over medium heat, frequently turning it, until browned well, and drain off any excess fat. Return the bacon to the Dutch oven along with the brown sugar mixture, water, and beer. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, covered, until the beef is tender – approximately 2 ½ to 3 hours, or transfer to a slow cooker and cook on low for 4 to 6 hours. If preparing later, keep the beef and broth separate and refrigerate for no more than 48 hours. To serve, about 45 minutes prior, skim any fat from the broth. (If using a slow cooker, add the stew vegetables during the final 1 ½ hours.) Bring the beef and broth to a boil, add the vegetables, and simmer until heated through and tender, around 20 minutes. Transfer the beef and vegetables to a warmed platter and thicken the gravy by whisking together 1 cup of cold water and 1/2 cup of all-purpose flour; gradually stir this slurry into the simmering broth, ensuring constant stirring, until it reaches a boil and thickens for one minute. Serve immediately with the beef and vegetables.

The payments were made over several years with the aim of securing power supply deals between Westinghouse Electric's subsidiary Atlantic Electric Power Corporation and the African government, which was looking for new suppliers. ProPublica reported that in one instance, a Westinghouse executive gave a gift of $700,000 in bribe money to a senior official in order to influence the outcome of bid negotiations. According to documents obtained by the two outlets, other officials were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by ATAC in exchange for recommending its equipment to government agencies and companies. The scheme was uncovered through a whistleblower who exposed the corruption to authorities. In response, the United States Department of Justice said Westinghouse would pay $364 million in fines, including criminal penalties for violating anti-bribery laws in relation to similar schemes in Peru and Colombia.

A book about the evolution of mutants and the science of abnormality has won the Guardian First Book Award 2004.
Armand Marie Leroi, a lecturer at London's Imperial College, scooped the £10,000 prize for Mutants: On the form, varieties and errors of the human body. "It is profoundly cultured and beautifully written in the very best tradition of popular science writing today," said judge Claire Armistead. The award recognises and rewards new writing across fiction and non-fiction. A panel of literary experts, including novelists Hari Kunzru and Ali Smith, director Sir Richard Eyre and comedian Alexei Sayle chose the winner from a five-strong shortlist.
The shortlist included Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange and Mr Norrell, a novel about the magic arts at the turn of the 19th Century and The Places In Between, Rory Stewart's account of his trek, on foot, across Afghanistan. "What we found so impressive about Armand Marie Leroi's book was the scope of its reference, its elegance and its inquisitiveness," said Ms Armistead, chair of the judges and the Guardian literary editor. "While the subject matter of Mutants unsettled some involved in the judging process, the overwhelming majority found it fascinating," she added. Her words were echoed by Iris director Sir Richard Eyre who called Marie Leroi's work "extraordinarily thought provoking". The award, for first time authors, is open to books from genres including fiction, poetry, biography, memoir, history, politics, science and current affairs. Previous winners include White Teeth by Zadie Smith, in 2000, which went on to become a bestseller.

Global aphasia is a severe form of aphasia, a language disorder that results from damage to portions of the brain responsible for language. It is characterized by a significant impairment in all aspects of language comprehension and production. Individuals with global aphasia have difficulty understanding spoken or written language, finding the right words to express themselves, and reading or writing.

Global aphasia is most commonly caused by a stroke, particularly in the left hemisphere of the brain, which is responsible for language and communication. Other potential causes include traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, infections, and degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's.

Symptoms of global aphasia can vary depending on the extent of brain damage. However, common symptoms include difficulty speaking or understanding speech, inability to read or write, and difficulty finding the right words. Some individuals may also experience physical difficulties such as weakness or paralysis on one side of the body.

Diagnosis of global aphasia is typically made through a series of language and cognitive tests conducted by a speech-language pathologist. These tests assess the individual's ability to understand, speak, read, and write. Brain imaging techniques such as MRI or CT scans may also be used to identify the location and extent of brain damage.

Treatment for global aphasia is usually centered around speech and language therapy. The goal of therapy is to improve the individual's ability to communicate by restoring as much language function as possible and teaching alternative methods of communication when necessary. The intensity and duration of therapy can vary depending on the severity of the aphasia.

The prognosis for individuals with global aphasia varies. Some individuals may make significant improvements, particularly with intensive speech and language therapy. However, others may continue to experience significant language difficulties. The extent of recovery is generally dependent on the size and location of the brain damage, the individual's age and health status, and the intensity of speech and language therapy.

Research into global aphasia is ongoing, with scientists seeking to better understand the brain mechanisms involved in language and communication, as well as develop more effective treatment strategies. Current research areas include the use of technology in aphasia therapy, the role of music therapy in language recovery, and the potential of certain medications to enhance language function.

In conclusion, global aphasia is a severe language disorder that significantly impacts an individual's ability to communicate. Despite the challenges it presents, many individuals with global aphasia are able to improve their communication skills with the help of speech and language therapy and other treatment strategies.

Japan's biggest bank, Mizuho Financial Group, has agreed to pay $1bn (£650m) in compensation and other costs after being accused by regulators of manipulating its benchmark interest rate for years. The deal will see the lender admit wrongdoing over its role in setting the Libor inter-bank lending rate between banks around the world. It also means that it will be forced to sell off assets worth more than $20bn. The settlement comes as Japan's financial regulator prepares to announce new rules on how banks should report their dealings with each other. The move could lead to further fines or even criminal charges against some of the country's largest lenders. The scandal erupted last year when Barclays was fined £290m for rigging Libor. But the Japanese government said it would not pursue any individual bankers involved in the scandal. Instead, it decided to settle with Mizuho, which had been accused of using its influence to help clients manipulate the rate. The bank admitted to having manipulated the rate since 2004. It paid $972m in penalties and $2.5bn in compensation. The settlement includes a provision for another $3.6bn in damages. Butter a 10" springform cake pan. First Layer: Crush 8 ounces of Oreo cookies. (I used my Cuisinart to crush them). Add 1/4 cup melted butter to the crumbs and pulse again. The high-fidelity storage of quantum information is crucial for quantum
computation and communication. Many experimental platforms for these
applications exhibit highly biased noise, with good resilience to spin
depolarisation undermined by high dephasing rates. In this work, we demonstrate
that the memory performance of a noise-biased trapped-ion qubit memory can be
greatly improved by incorporating error correction of dephasing errors through
teleportation of the information between two repetition codes written on a pair
of qubit registers in the same trap. While the technical requirements of error
correction are often considerable, we show that our protocol can be achieved
with a single global entangling phase gate of remarkably low fidelity,
leveraging the fact that the gate errors are also dominated by dephasing-type
processes. By rebalancing the logical spin-flip and dephasing error rates, we
show that for realistic parameters our memory can exhibit error rates up to two
orders of magnitude lower than the unprotected physical qubits, thus providing
a useful means of improving memory performance in trapped ion systems where
field-insensitive qubits are not available.

Deep image segmentation is a long-standing key challenge in computer vision. Initially, many algorithms were unsupervised, relying on manually defined characteristics to segment images into distinct areas. More recently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have dramatically improved segmentation accuracy; nevertheless, these approaches typically require extensive labeled data, making annotation costly. This paper introduces a new deep unsupervised segmentation technique comprised of two main steps. Firstly, a Superpixelwise Autoencoder (SuperAE) learns a rich feature representation and generates a smoother version of the input image. Subsequently, a novel clustering approach, termed Deep Superpixel Cut (DSC), calculates deep similarities between superpixels and utilizes them to perform flexible image partitioning through a process of adaptive division via backpropagation. Evaluations using the BSDS500 dataset confirm the efficacy of our proposed method.

Extracting a connectome from an electron microscopy (EM) data set requires
identification of neurons and determination of synapses between neurons. As
manual extraction of this information is very time-consuming, there has been
extensive research effort to automatically segment the neurons to help guide
and eventually replace manual tracing. Until recently, there has been
comparatively less research on automatically detecting the actual synapses
between neurons. This discrepancy can, in part, be attributed to several
factors: obtaining neuronal shapes is a prerequisite first step in extracting a
connectome, manual tracing is much more time-consuming than annotating
synapses, and neuronal contact area can be used as a proxy for synapses in
determining connections.
  However, recent research has demonstrated that contact area alone is not a
sufficient predictor of synaptic connection. Moreover, as segmentation has
improved, we have observed that synapse annotation is consuming a more
significant fraction of overall reconstruction time. This ratio will only get
worse as segmentation improves, gating overall possible speed-up. Therefore, we
address this problem by developing algorithms that automatically detect
pre-synaptic neurons and their post-synaptic partners. In particular,
pre-synaptic structures are detected using a Deep and Wide Multiscale Recursive
Network, and post-synaptic partners are detected using a MLP with features
conditioned on the local segmentation.
  This work is novel because it requires minimal amount of training, leverages
advances in image segmentation directly, and provides a complete solution for
polyadic synapse detection. We further introduce novel metrics to evaluate our
algorithm on connectomes of meaningful size. These metrics demonstrate that
complete automatic prediction can be used to effectively characterize most
connectivity correctly.

> We study the effect of Coulomb repulsion on the dynamics and yields of linear coasting nucleosynthesis (LCN). In LCN, the expansion rate of the plasma is much slower than that of the baryon-free radiation fluid, so that the baryons are dragged along by the latter. This leads to an effective cooling of the baryonic matter which can be used as a mechanism to produce light elements such as 4He or D during Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) or primordial black holes (PBHs) after inflation. However, this process has been shown to fail when the number density of baryons becomes too large due to the strong Coulomb interaction between protons and electrons. Here we show how the inclusion of Coulomb screening effects allows one to extend the range of validity of LCN up to densities where the standard BBN scenario applies. As a result, it is possible to obtain a significant amount of deuterium production at temperatures below the QCD phase transition without violating any observational constraints.

Segmenting images of low quality or with missing data is a challenging
problem. Integrating statistical prior information about the shapes to be
segmented can improve the segmentation results significantly. Most shape-based
segmentation algorithms optimize an energy functional and find a point estimate
for the object to be segmented. This does not provide a measure of the degree
of confidence in that result, neither does it provide a picture of other
probable solutions based on the data and the priors. With a statistical view,
addressing these issues would involve the problem of characterizing the
posterior densities of the shapes of the objects to be segmented. For such
characterization, we propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling-based
image segmentation algorithm that uses statistical shape priors. In addition to
better characterization of the statistical structure of the problem, such an
approach would also have the potential to address issues with getting stuck at
local optima, suffered by existing shape-based segmentation methods. Our
approach is able to characterize the posterior probability density in the space
of shapes through its samples, and to return multiple solutions, potentially
from different modes of a multimodal probability density, which would be
encountered, e.g., in segmenting objects from multiple shape classes. We
present promising results on a variety of data sets. We also provide an
extension for segmenting shapes of objects with parts that can go through
independent shape variations. This extension involves the use of local shape
priors on object parts and provides robustness to limitations in shape training
data size.

If your period is delayed, it can be incredibly stressful and worrying. There are many factors that can cause a period to be late, including hormonal changes, stress, and other medical conditions. Here are some tips to help manage your concerns:
1. Wait - Sometimes a period can be up to two weeks late and still considered normal. If you're anxious about it, try distracting yourself with something fun or relaxing until you get your next period.
2. Keep track - Track when you expect your period typically starts and ends so you can better keep track if it's running late. This will also allow you to notice any patterns or potential issues more quickly.
3. Call for backup - Contact your healthcare provider right away if your period has been absent for over typical time frame. They may recommend further testing or treatment options based on the cause.
4. Take care of yourself - Make sure you're eating well, exercising regularly, getting enough sleep and managing stress levels because these factors can affect your menstrual cycle.
Remember, everyone's body is unique and there can be many reasons why periods run late. Don't let worry get in the way of enjoying life. Seek professional advice if you need to and try to stay positive and relaxed during this trying times.

Remember, you deserve to be happy and healthy. Lean into that feeling and know that you made the right decision for your own well-being.

Economists predict that an increase is unlikely to come until the second half of 2005, with growth set to sputter rather than ignite.
"During 2004 we profited from the fact that the world economy was strong," said Stefan Schilbe, analyst at HSBC Trinkaus & Burkhardt.
