Born in New York City on May 16, 1959, Andrew Litton is an American orchestral conductor. He attended The Fieldston School before studying piano with Nadia Reisenberg and conducting with Sixten Ehrling at Juilliard, earning degrees in both disciplines. His training further extended to Salzburg Mozarteum with Walter Weller and Edoardo Müller. Early influences included John DeMaio. A young victor of the BBC International Conductors Competition in 1982, Litton held positions as Assistant Conductor at Teatro alla Scala and with the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington, D.C., under Mstislav Rostropovich (1982-1985), progressing to Associate Conductor (1985-1986). He participated in the Exxon-Arts Endowment Conductors Program and received Yale University’s Sanford Medal in 2003. Litton began his conducting career with the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra, leading them as principal conductor from 1988 to 1994, and currently holds the title of conductor laureate. He then directed the Dallas Symphony Orchestra for twelve years, from 1994 to 2006, later becoming Music Director Emeritus. From 2003 to 2017, he oversaw artistic programming for the Sommerfest concerts of the Minnesota Orchestra.

Residual amplitude modulation (RAM) within laser interferometers employing heterodyne sensing can have significant and challenging consequences. Here, we investigate RAM’s impact on a sophisticated laser interferometer designed for gravitational wave detection. RAM generates spurious adjustments within the cavity length measurements, altering the operational position of the optical cavities through feedback and causing fluctuations in the sensor matrix. These changes degrade the precision noise subtraction employed by the multi-degree-of-freedom control system. Furthermore, these detuned cavities create an optomechanical spring, further modifying the sensor matrix. Our simulations reveal necessary RAM levels for future Advanced LIGO detectors, demonstrating that anticipated RAM levels won't compromise the detector's sensitivity.

ITP3K, or inositol (1,4,5) trisphosphate 3-kinase, is an enzyme involved in transferring phosphate groups from ATP to 1D-myo-inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate. Classified as a phosphotransferase within the transferase family, it works by adding a phosphorus moiety to inositol. Specifically, ITP3K catalyzes the reaction forming inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate by transferring gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 3-position of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), resulting in the production of Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, also called inositol tetrakisphosphate or IP4. Various names and abbreviations are used for this enzyme, including 1D-myo-inositol-trisphosphate 3-kinase, ITP3K, ITPK, IP3-kinase, IP3-3-kinase, and Ins(1,4,5)P3 3-kinase. Its genes include ITPKA, ITPKB, and ITPKC in humans, and IP3K1 and IP3K2 in fruit flies (known as “wavy” mutants). A single version of the enzyme exists in nematodes, encoded by the LFE-2 gene. Importantly, ITP3K expression is limited to metazoans – it’s absent in yeast and plants.

Brazilian Coconut Beijinhos are a delicious and easy-to-make Brazilian dessert. They are made with just a few simple ingredients, including sweetened condensed milk, butter, and coconut. Here is a recipe for Brazilian Coconut Beijinhos:

Ingredients:

- 1 can (14 oz) sweetened condensed milk
- 1/2 cup (1 stick) butter, melted
- 2 cups coconut, finely shredded
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 2 eggs
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

Instructions:

1. Preheat oven to 350°F (180°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a large bowl, combine sweetened condensed milk, melted butter, coconut, baking powder, and salt. Stir in flour until well combined.
3. Add eggs and vanilla extract, and mix until well combined.
4. Roll dough into 1-inch balls and place on prepared baking sheet.
5. Bake for 20-25 minutes, or until lightly browned.
6. Let cool on wire rack for 5 minutes before serving.

Pork Chops with Apples and Pancetta Recipe

Ingredients:
- 4 pork chops, thick-cut
- Salt and pepper
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 8 ounces pancetta, diced
- 2 large apples, cored and sliced
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- 1/4 cup chicken broth
- 2 tablespoons butter

Instructions:

1. Preheat oven to 400°F.
2. Season the pork chops with salt and pepper on both sides.
3. Heat the olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat. Add the pork chops and cook for 3-4 minutes on each side until nicely browned. Remove the pork chops from the skillet and set aside.
4. Add the diced pancetta to the same skillet and cook over medium heat until crispy, about 5-7 minutes.
5. Add the sliced apples, minced garlic, and dried thyme to the skillet. Cook for 2-3 minutes until the apples start to soften.
6. Pour in the chicken broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.
7. Place the pork chops back into the skillet, spooning some of the apple and pancetta mixture on top of the pork chops.
8. Dot the top of the apples with butter and bake in the preheated oven for 20-25 minutes until the pork chops are fully cooked and the apples are tender.
9. Serve the pork chops with apples and pancetta hot, garnished with fresh thyme if desired. Enjoy!

To prepare these coconut porcupine buns, you’ll need 250 grams of bread flour, 6 grams of sugar, 1 teaspoon of olive oil, 130 milliliters of water, 5 grams of active dry yeast, 1/2 teaspoon of salt, 50 milliliters of coconut syrup (treacle or corn syrup), 1/4 teaspoon of cinnamon powder, 1/2 teaspoon of sugar, and 100 grams of desiccated coconut. First, sift the flour and combine it with the remaining ingredients in a bowl, mixing for approximately one minute. Add the olive oil and water, then knead the dough by hand for about 10 minutes on a lightly floured surface. Allow the dough to rest, covered, in a warm spot for 30 minutes. Then, divide the dough into 15 lemon-sized balls. Roll each ball out into a 2 1/2-inch diameter disk, ¼ inch thick. For the coconut topping, heat coconut syrup, cinnamon, and sugar in a saucepan until it reaches 100°C. Combine this mixture with the desiccated coconut and let it cool. Spoon a teaspoon of the cooled coconut mixture onto the center of each disk, roll them into balls, and shape them into oval forms. Use scissors to create prickly “porcupine” shapes at the top. Place the buns on oiled parchment paper, steam them over simmering water for about 10 minutes. Once cooked, remove from the steamer and decorate with eyes (using food coloring), a mouth, and whiskers made from coir (coconut husk). Serve warm. Shares in US phone company MCI have risen on speculation that it is in takeover talks.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Qwest has bid $6.3bn (£3.4bn) for MCI. Other firms have also expressed an interest in MCI, the second-largest US long-distance phone firm, and may now table rival bids, analysts said. Shares in MCI, which changed its name from Worldcom when it emerged from bankruptcy, were up 2.4% at $20.15. Press reports suggest that Qwest and MCI may reach an agreement as early as next week, although rival bids may muddy the waters. The largest US telephone company Verizon has previously held preliminary merger discussions with MCI, Reuters quoted sources as saying.
Consolidation in the US telecommunications industry has picked up in the past few months as companies look to cut costs and boost client bases. A merger between MCI and Qwest would be the fifth billion-dollar telecoms deal since October. Last week, SBC Communications agreed to buy its former parent and phone trailblazer AT&T for about $16bn. Competition has intensified and fixed-line phone providers such as MCI and AT&T have seen themselves overtaken by rivals. Buying MCI would give Qwest, a local phone service provider, access to MCI's global network and business-based subscribers. MCI also offers internet services.
MCI was renamed after it emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in April last year. It hit the headlines as Worldcom in 2002 after admitting it illegally booked expenses and inflated profits. The scandal was a key factor in a global slide in share prices and the reverberations are still being felt today. Shareholders lost about $180bn when the company collapsed, while 20,000 workers lost their jobs. Former Worldcom boss Bernie Ebbers is currently on trial, accused of overseeing an $11bn fraud.
